Applied Bayesian Inference · Chapter 11

Chapter 11
Unsupervised models

Lectures 21–23 · latent factors behind questionnaires, mixtures behind measurements, the posteriors that will not agree with themselves, and copulas that separate dependence from the margins

Every chapter so far has had an outcome: something the model was asked to predict or explain. This chapter drops it. We are left with a table of measurements and no label, and the question is whether the table itself contains structure: a few underlying dimensions along which people or objects vary, or a few groups into which they fall. Both kinds of structure are latent, never observed directly, and both are inferred by the same Bayesian machinery as before: write down a model in which the latent structure generates the data, and compute the posterior.

  • Lecture 21 is about latent factors. A personality questionnaire asks 25 questions; psychologists claim the answers reflect five underlying traits. We build principal components, probabilistic PCA and the factor model, fit a Bayesian factor model in Stan, meet the rotation problem, and ask how many factors the data actually support.
  • Lecture 22 is about mixtures. We hide the species labels of the Palmer penguins from Chapter 1 and ask whether four body measurements can find the species again. Along the way we meet label switching, a posterior that will not agree with itself, soft assignments, and the Dirichlet process, and then we look for breast-cancer subtypes in expression data.
  • Lecture 23 is about copulas. Two genes can be strongly correlated in very different ways. We separate a joint distribution into its margins and its dependence with Sklar's theorem, meet the main copula families and their tails, fit them in Stan to co-amplified genes, use the Gaussian copula for questionnaires that mix ordinal, binary and continuous answers, and check whether home and away goals in football are independent.

Think About It: Before You Start

Suppose a clustering algorithm splits a set of patients into three groups. What would convince you that the groups are real, rather than a partition the algorithm would have produced from any data? And if a patient sits halfway between two groups, should the algorithm say so, or assign her to one of them? Keep your answers in mind; Lecture 22 is built around them.

Lecture 21 — Latent factors

11.1 Twenty-five questions

The Synthetic Aperture Personality Assessment project (SAPA) collected answers to personality items from thousands of volunteers online. William Revelle distributes 2,800 of them as the bfi data set (Revelle, 2024): 25 statements, five for each of the "Big Five" personality traits (Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Neuroticism and Openness), each rated on a six-point scale from "very inaccurate" to "very accurate" as a description of oneself. "I am indifferent to the feelings of others" (A1), "I am exacting in my work" (C1), "I make friends easily" (E4), "I get angry easily" (N1), "I am full of ideas" (O1). Some statements are worded in reverse, so that agreeing indicates less of the trait; we reverse their scores so that every item points the same way.

The questions: do 25 answers really record 25 different things, or a handful of underlying dimensions? If a handful, how many, and what are they? Psychology's answer, the five-factor model, was itself found largely by factor analysis of questionnaires like this one. Here we ask whether a Bayesian factor model applied to these data agrees.

R
library(tidyverse)
library(rstan)
library(loo)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

harbour <- c(ink = "#10191d", muted = "#4a5f68", grid = "#d5e3e6",
             sky = "#1d5187", amber = "#805907", rose = "#ad3b28",
             moss = "#1d6b54", lilac = "#5b3a94")
theme_harbour <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(text = element_text(colour = harbour[["ink"]]),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = harbour[["muted"]]),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = harbour[["grid"]]),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(colour = harbour[["ink"]], hjust = 0),
          legend.position = "top")
}
theme_set(theme_harbour())
R
tmp <- tempfile()
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cran/psychTools/master/data/bfi.rda", tmp, quiet = TRUE)
load(tmp)                                                   # creates `bfi`
reversed <- c("A1", "C4", "C5", "E1", "E2", "O2", "O5")     # negatively worded items
items <- bfi |> select(A1:O5) |> drop_na() |> mutate(across(all_of(reversed), ~ 7 - .x))
Y <- scale(as.matrix(items))                                # standardised: correlations, not raw scores
c(people = nrow(Y), items = ncol(Y))
round(cor(items)[c("N1", "N2", "E1", "E4", "C2"), c("N1", "N2", "E1", "E4", "C2")], 2)
output
people  items 
  2436     25 
      N1    N2    E1    E4    C2
N1  1.00  0.72 -0.01 -0.14 -0.02
N2  0.72  1.00 -0.02 -0.15 -0.01
E1 -0.01 -0.02  1.00  0.42 -0.02
E4 -0.14 -0.15  0.42  1.00  0.12
C2 -0.02 -0.01 -0.02  0.12  1.00

After dropping people with any missing answer, 2,436 of the 2,800 remain. The correlations show the pattern factor analysis looks for. Two Neuroticism items correlate 0.72 with each other and two Extraversion items 0.42, while items written for different traits correlate between −0.15 and 0.12. Items written for the same trait hang together; items written for different traits mostly do not.

11.2 Latent variables as causes

The factor model makes a causal claim, and it is worth stating it before fitting anything. A person has a level of neuroticism, which we cannot observe. That level causes her answers to "I get angry easily", "I get irritated easily" and "I panic easily". The five Neuroticism answers are correlated because they share a cause, and once the cause is known they are independent: this is local independence, the fork of Chapter 1 with an unobserved common cause.

This direction is an assumption, not a finding. Psychometricians call it a reflective model: the items reflect the trait. The alternative is a formative model, in which the items cause the construct: socioeconomic status is made up of income, education and occupation, and a rise in income raises status without any common cause behind it. A factor model fitted to formative indicators will happily find a "factor", because correlated variables always have a first principal axis, but that factor is a summary, not a cause, and interventions on it make no sense. A second warning applies to both: the latent variable is defined by the model. If we had asked different questions, we would have found different factors. The Big Five are a description of what people say about themselves in English-language questionnaires, and whether they are also causal entities in the brain is a question no factor analysis can settle (Borsboom, Mellenbergh and van Heerden, 2003).

Check Yourself

A hospital builds a "frailty index" from 30 indicators: number of chronic diseases, walking speed, grip strength, need for help with dressing, and so on. Should it be analysed with a reflective factor model?

Correlation alone does not tell you which way the arrows run.

Factor models can be useful even when they are not causal, but the interpretation changes.

Correlated indicators are compatible with a common cause, with indicators that cause each other (chronic disease causes slow walking), and with an index that is merely their sum. The factor model assumes the first. Both a frailty "phenotype" (Fried et al., 2001) and a "deficit index" (Mitnitski, Mogilner and Rockwood, 2001) are in use. Reading the first as reflective and the second as formative is our gloss rather than a settled classification, but it shows what each one assumes.

It depends on the causal story. If frailty is thought to be an underlying state that produces slow walking and weak grip, a reflective model fits. If frailty is simply defined as the accumulation of deficits, the indicators form the index and a factor model's "frailty" would be a summary, not a cause; local independence would then have no reason to hold.

11.3 From principal components to factors

Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions in the 25-dimensional space of answers along which people vary most. Mathematically, these are the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix, and each eigenvalue is the variance along its direction. No probability model is involved. If the five-trait story is right, we expect five eigenvalues to stand out and the other twenty to be small and similar.

R
ev <- eigen(cor(Y))$values
tibble(component = 1:10, eigenvalue = round(ev[1:10], 2),
       cumulative_share = round(cumsum(ev)[1:10] / sum(ev), 3))
output
# A tibble: 10 x 3
   component eigenvalue cumulative_share
       <int>      <dbl>            <dbl>
 1         1       5.13            0.205
 2         2       2.75            0.315
 3         3       2.14            0.401
 4         4       1.85            0.475
 5         5       1.55            0.537
 6         6       1.07            0.58 
 7         7       0.84            0.614
 8         8       0.8             0.646
 9         9       0.72            0.674
10        10       0.69            0.702

Five eigenvalues stand clearly above 1 (5.13, 2.75, 2.14, 1.85 and 1.55), the sixth is 1.07, and from the seventh on they decline slowly from 0.84. Together the first five components account for 54% of the variance in the 25 items. That supports a handful of dimensions, and five is a reasonable reading, though the cut-off is not sharp: the classical rule of keeping eigenvalues above 1 would say six. Notice too that the first eigenvalue is much larger than the rest; the rotation widget below shows why.

Probabilistic PCA (Tipping and Bishop, 1999) turns this into a generative model. Each person i has a vector of K latent scores fi∼Normal(0,IK), and her standardised answers are a noisy linear function of them:

yi=Λfi+εi,εi∼Normal(0, Ψ).

The 25×K matrix Λ holds the loadings: Λjk says how strongly factor k drives item j. In probabilistic PCA the noise has the same variance for every item, Ψ=σ2I; in the factor analysis model each item has its own unique variance ψj2, the part of the answer that the factors do not explain. Integrating out the unobserved fi gives the distribution of the data:

yi∼Normal(0, ΛΛ⊤+Ψ).

All the information about the factors is in the covariance matrix: the model says that 300 correlations between 25 items are generated by 25K loadings and 25 unique variances. It also says something uncomfortable. If R is any K×K rotation matrix (RR⊤=I), then (ΛR)(ΛR)⊤=ΛΛ⊤: rotated loadings fit the data exactly as well. The likelihood cannot tell a factor model from any rotation of itself. The widget shows this with two factors.

Rotating two factors

The loadings of the 25 items on a two-factor model fitted to these data (posterior means), coloured by the trait each item was written for. Rotating the axes changes every loading but not the correlations the model implies: the readout shows the largest change in any implied correlation (always zero). The varimax button picks the rotation that makes loadings most nearly "simple": each item large on one factor and near zero on the other.

At 0° the plot shows the solution as fitted, with the loadings constrained to lower-triangular form and E3 and N1 as anchors (Section 11.4 explains the constraint). Because the anchors are strong items of two different traits, this solution is already close to simple structure, and the varimax button moves it by only about a degree: the Neuroticism items lie along factor 2, and the Extraversion and Agreeableness items, with the weaker Conscientiousness and Openness items, along factor 1. That so many items load positively on one direction is why the first eigenvalue is so large. Now rotate by 45°: every item loads on both factors and the picture is hard to read, yet the readout shows that nothing about the fit has changed. Rotation is a choice made for interpretation, and the varimax criterion (Kaiser, 1958), which maximises the variance of the squared loadings within each factor, is one convention for making it.

11.4 A Bayesian factor model

For a Bayesian fit, the rotation problem is more than cosmetic. If the likelihood is unchanged along a continuum of rotations, so is the posterior (with rotation-invariant priors), and the sampler wanders around a ridge of equally good solutions; the chains never agree and the loadings have no meaningful posterior mean. The standard fix (Geweke and Zhou, 1996) is to choose one representative from each set of rotations: constrain Λ to be lower triangular with a positive diagonal. Item 1 loads only on factor 1, item 2 only on factors 1 and 2, and so on up to item K; from item K+1 on, all loadings are free. Any Λ can be rotated into this form, so the constraint restricts the parameterisation, not the fit. The first K items are called anchors.

Because the model depends on the data only through the sample covariance matrix S, the likelihood can be computed from S in one step rather than person by person: for N people, log⁡p(Y)=−N2[log⁡|Σ|+tr(Σ−1S)] plus a constant, with Σ=ΛΛ⊤+Ψ. That makes the model fast even for thousands of respondents. We still compute each person's log-likelihood in generated quantities, for leave-one-out comparison.

R
fa_code <- "
data { int<lower=1> N; int<lower=1> P; int<lower=1> K; matrix[N, P] Y; }
transformed data { matrix[P, P] S = crossprod(Y) / N; }   // sample covariance (Y is centred)
parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[K] ldiag;                         // positive diagonal of the loadings
  vector[K * (K - 1) / 2 + (P - K) * K] lfree;      // loadings below the diagonal
  vector<lower=0>[P] psi;                           // unique standard deviations
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[P, K] L = rep_matrix(0, P, K);             // lower triangular: identifies the rotation
  { int idx = 1;
    for (j in 1:K) { L[j, j] = ldiag[j];
      for (i in (j + 1):P) { L[i, j] = lfree[idx]; idx += 1; } } }
}
model {
  matrix[P, P] Sigma = add_diag(tcrossprod(L), square(psi));
  ldiag ~ normal(0, 1); lfree ~ normal(0, 1); psi ~ exponential(1);
  target += -0.5 * N * (log_determinant(Sigma) + trace(mdivide_left_spd(Sigma, S)));
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  { matrix[P, P] Lc = cholesky_decompose(add_diag(tcrossprod(L), square(psi)));
    for (n in 1:N) log_lik[n] = multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf(Y[n]' | rep_vector(0, P), Lc); }
}"
fa_mod <- stan_model(model_code = fa_code)

Which items should be the anchors? This matters more than the theory suggests. The constraint forces anchor k to load positively on factor k, so an anchor that barely relates to the factor we hope it defines leaves the posterior with two nearly equal modes, one for each sign, and chains can settle in different ones. In a first attempt (before reverse-scoring the negatively worded items, and with anchors chosen by hand), one chain found a solution in which the "Agreeableness" anchor had a loading of 0.01 while the other found 0.41, and R^ reached 37. The cure is to choose, for each factor, the item that loads most strongly on it in a quick classical solution (maximum-likelihood factor analysis with factanal()), and to start every chain at that classical solution rotated into lower-triangular form.

R
fit_fa <- function(K) {
  path <- sprintf("fits/ch11_fa%d.rds", K); if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  ml <- factanal(Y, K, rotation = if (K > 1) "varimax" else "none")    # classical solution
  Lml <- unclass(ml$loadings); anchors <- integer(0)
  for (j in 1:K) { a <- abs(Lml[, j]); a[anchors] <- -1; anchors <- c(anchors, which.max(a)) }
  ord <- c(anchors, setdiff(seq_len(ncol(Y)), anchors))              # anchors first
  Lm <- Lml[ord, , drop = FALSE]
  Q <- qr.Q(qr(t(Lm[1:K, , drop = FALSE])))                          # rotate to lower-triangular form
  Li <- Lm %*% Q; Li <- sweep(Li, 2, sign(diag(Li[1:K, , drop = FALSE])), "*")
  init <- function() list(ldiag = as.array(diag(Li[1:K, , drop = FALSE])),
                          lfree = as.array(unlist(lapply(1:K, function(j) Li[(j + 1):ncol(Y), j]))),
                          psi = sqrt(ml$uniquenesses[ord]))
  fit <- sampling(fa_mod, data = list(N = nrow(Y), P = ncol(Y), K = K, Y = Y[, ord]),
                  chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 11, refresh = 0, init = init)
  out <- list(fit = fit, items = colnames(Y)[ord]); saveRDS(out, path); out
}
fa5 <- fit_fa(5)
fa5$items[1:5]                                           # the anchors
s5 <- summary(fa5$fit, pars = c("ldiag", "lfree", "psi"))$summary
c(max_rhat = round(max(s5[, "Rhat"]), 3), min_ess = round(min(s5[, "n_eff"])),
  divergences = get_num_divergent(fa5$fit))
output
[1] "N1" "E2" "C4" "A3" "O3"
   max_rhat     min_ess divergences 
       1.01      953.00        0.00

The anchors chosen from the classical solution are N1 ("Get angry easily"), E2 ("Find it difficult to approach others", reverse-scored), C4 ("Do things in a half-way manner", reverse-scored), A3 ("Know how to comfort others") and O3 ("Carry the conversation to a higher level"). Started from the classical solution, the four chains agree: the largest R^ is 1.01, the smallest effective sample size is 953, and there are no divergent transitions. The fit takes under a minute.

The lower-triangular loadings are identified but not interpretable: they depend on which items we chose as anchors. To read the factors, we rotate. We take the varimax rotation of the posterior mean loadings as a reference, and then rotate every posterior draw to match the reference as closely as possible (an orthogonal Procrustes rotation, one singular value decomposition per draw). Because rotation does not change the fit, every rotated draw is an equally valid draw from the posterior; we have only chosen how to look at it.

R
rotate_draws <- function(res) {
  L <- rstan::extract(res$fit, "L")$L                        # draws x items x factors
  ref <- unclass(varimax(apply(L, c(2, 3), mean))$loadings)
  key <- substr(res$items[apply(abs(ref), 2, which.max)], 1, 1)  # trait letter of each factor's top item
  ref <- sweep(ref, 2, sign(ref[cbind(apply(abs(ref), 2, which.max), seq_len(ncol(ref)))]), "*")
  rot <- apply(L, 1, function(M) { sv <- svd(crossprod(M, ref)); M %*% sv$u %*% t(sv$v) })
  rot <- array(t(rot), dim(L)); dimnames(rot) <- list(NULL, res$items, key); rot
}
lam <- rotate_draws(fa5)
lam_tab <- as.data.frame.table(apply(lam, c(2, 3), mean), responseName = "mean") |>
  bind_cols(lo = as.vector(apply(lam, c(2, 3), quantile, 0.05)),
            hi = as.vector(apply(lam, c(2, 3), quantile, 0.95))) |>
  rename(item = Var1, factor = Var2) |> mutate(trait = substr(item, 1, 1))
lam_tab |> group_by(factor) |> slice_max(abs(mean), n = 3) |> mutate(across(c(mean, lo, hi), ~ round(.x, 2)))
output

 2 N2    N       0.79  0.76  0.82 N    
 3 N3    N       0.72  0.69  0.75 N    
 4 E2    E       0.68  0.64  0.71 E    
 5 E4    E       0.62  0.59  0.65 E    
 6 E1    E       0.59  0.55  0.63 E

After rotation, each factor is led by the items of one trait, so we can name the factors N, E, C, A and O. The strongest loadings are those of N1 and N2 on Neuroticism (0.82 and 0.79), E2 on Extraversion (0.68), C4 on Conscientiousness (0.66), A3 on Agreeableness (0.66) and O3 on Openness (0.62). The 90% intervals are narrow, about ±0.03: with 2,436 people, the loadings are well determined once the rotation is fixed. The names are ours, not the model's. The model found five directions, and we named them after the items that load on them.

R
lam_tab |> mutate(item = fct_rev(factor(item)), big = abs(mean) > 0.3) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = item)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = harbour[["grid"]]) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, colour = big), height = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean, colour = big), size = 1.3) +
  facet_grid(trait ~ factor, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(factor = function(x) paste("factor", x))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = harbour[["muted"]], `TRUE` = harbour[["sky"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.4, 0.8)) + labs(x = "loading", y = NULL)

Every item loads most strongly on the factor of its own trait, so the five-factor structure is recovered. But it is not perfectly simple. The largest cross-loadings link Extraversion and Agreeableness: E4 ("Make friends easily") loads 0.36 on Agreeableness, and A5 ("Make people feel at ease") 0.36 on Extraversion. N4 ("Often feel blue") loads −0.37 on Extraversion, so it measures low mood as much as emotional reactivity. O4 ("Spend time reflecting on things") is the weakest Openness item (0.37), with small loadings on Neuroticism (0.21) and, negatively, Extraversion (−0.22). Departures like these are what a sixth or seventh factor can absorb.

Check Yourself

An item has standardised loadings 0.6 on one factor and 0 on all others, and the factors are uncorrelated with variance 1. What share of the item's variance do the factors explain (its communality)?

The item's variance is ∑kΛjk2+ψj2=1 for a standardised item.

The communality is ∑kΛjk2=0.62=0.36, so 36% of the variance in answers to this item is shared with the other items through the factor, and the unique variance ψj2=0.64 is the rest: specific content of the question plus measurement error. Loadings of 0.5 to 0.7 are typical of personality items, which is why single questions are poor measures of a trait and questionnaires use several.

11.5 How many factors?

Five factors was the theory's choice. The data can be asked, too: fit models with K=1,…,8 and compare their expected log predictive density by PSIS-LOO, which here measures how well each model predicts a new person's 25 answers.

R
fits_k <- map(1:8, fit_fa)
loos_k <- map(fits_k, ~ loo(extract_log_lik(.x$fit)))
cmp <- map_dfr(1:8, function(k) {
  d <- loos_k[[k]]$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - loos_k[[5]]$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
  tibble(K = k, diff = sum(d), se = sqrt(length(d)) * sd(d),
         max_rhat = max(summary(fits_k[[k]]$fit, pars = c("ldiag", "psi"))$summary[, "Rhat"]))
})
ggplot(cmp, aes(K, diff)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = harbour[["muted"]], linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = diff - 2 * se, ymax = diff + 2 * se), colour = harbour[["sky"]], size = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = harbour[["sky"]]) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "number of factors K", y = "elpd difference from K = 5")
cmp |> mutate(across(c(diff, se), ~ round(.x, 1)), max_rhat = round(max_rhat, 3))
L2 <- apply(rstan::extract(fits_k[[2]]$fit, "L")$L, c(2, 3), mean); items2 <- fits_k[[2]]$items
rm(fits_k, loos_k); invisible(gc())                      # free memory before compiling the next model
output
# A tibble: 8 x 4
      K   diff    se max_rhat
  <int>  <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1     1 -4486  138.      1   
2     2 -2482. 102       1   
3     3 -1461.  75.2     1.00
4     4  -728.  57       1.00
5     5     0    0       1.00
6     6   277.  32.4     1.00
7     7   395.  39       1.00
8     8   463.  42.4     1.01

LOO does not stop at five. Each extra factor up to five improves the expected log predictive density by hundreds or thousands of units, and beyond five the gains shrink but stay much larger than their standard errors: +277 for six factors, +395 for seven and +463 for eight, with standard errors from 32 to 42. All eight fits mixed well (largest R^ 1.01). With 2,436 people, small departures from the five-factor model become detectable: pairs of items with similar wording, items that belong partly to two traits, and six-point answers that are not normally distributed. A sixth or seventh factor may describe these better without being a new personality trait. LOO answers the question "which model predicts a new person's answers best?", and its answer is "more than five factors". Whether the extra factors are psychology or artefact is a substantive question, and Exercise 1 looks at what five factors miss.

History: From g to the Big Five

Factor analysis began with Charles Spearman (1904), who noticed that schoolchildren's marks in Classics, French, English and mathematics were all positively correlated, and proposed a single "general intelligence", g, as their common cause. Louis Thurstone (1935, 1947) generalised the method to several factors, invented the idea of rotation to "simple structure", and argued against Spearman that intelligence was several primary abilities; the dispute, a disagreement about rotation as much as about minds, ran for decades. Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert (1936) extracted about 18,000 personality-describing words from an English dictionary, on the "lexical hypothesis" that important differences between people become words. Factor analyses of ratings using such words kept producing five broad factors (Tupes and Christal in 1961, Norman in 1963, Goldberg in the 1980s), and by the 1990s the "Big Five" had become psychology's standard description of personality. Probabilistic PCA (Tipping and Bishop, 1999) and Bayesian PCA (Bishop, 1999) brought the same models into machine learning, where they are the simplest members of a family that runs through variational autoencoders.

Key Takeaways: Lecture 21

  • A factor model says that correlated observations share unobserved causes: y=Λf+ε, with local independence given f. The causal direction is an assumption; for formative indices it is wrong.
  • Loadings are identified only up to rotation. A Bayesian fit needs a constraint, such as lower-triangular loadings with positive diagonal, and the choice of anchor items matters: weak anchors create competing modes.
  • Start the chains from a classical solution, check R^, then rotate every draw (varimax plus Procrustes alignment) for interpretation.
  • Predictive comparisons with large samples keep rewarding extra factors; the number to report is a substantive decision informed, not dictated, by LOO.

Lecture 22 — Mixtures

11.6 Penguins without labels

In Chapter 1 we used the Palmer penguins (Gorman, Williams and Fraser, 2014; Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020) to predict body mass. Now we hide the one variable a biologist would never be without, the species, and ask whether four measurements (bill length, bill depth, flipper length and body mass) can find it again. The question is a fair test of clustering, because we know the answer: 151 Adélie, 68 Chinstrap and 123 Gentoo penguins, measured on three islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, between 2007 and 2009.

R
library(palmerpenguins)
birds <- penguins |> drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
Yp <- scale(as.matrix(select(birds, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)))
colnames(Yp) <- c("bill_length", "bill_depth", "flipper", "mass")
c(penguins = nrow(Yp), measurements = ncol(Yp))
output
    penguins measurements 
         342            4

A mixture model says that each penguin belongs to one of K unobserved groups, zi∈{1,…,K}, with probabilities w1,…,wK, and that its measurements are drawn from a distribution specific to its group:

zi∼Categorical(w),yi∣zi=k∼Normal(μk, Σk).

The group labels zi are discrete, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo cannot sample discrete parameters. As with the missing data of Chapter 7, the remedy is to sum them out: the likelihood of one penguin is

p(yi∣w,μ,Σ)=∑k=1KwkNormal(yi∣μk,Σk),

which depends only on continuous parameters. Each penguin's group is then recovered after fitting by Bayes' rule, draw by draw:

Pr(zi=k∣yi,w,μ,Σ)=wkNormal(yi∣μk,Σk)∑jwjNormal(yi∣μj,Σj).

Averaging over the posterior gives each penguin a soft assignment: a probability for each group, not a single label. Before HMC, mixtures were fitted by two older algorithms that are still worth knowing. The EM algorithm (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977) alternates between computing these membership probabilities (the E step) and re-estimating each group's weight, mean and variance from the penguins weighted by their memberships (the M step); it climbs to a local maximum of the likelihood. Gibbs sampling (Diebolt and Robert, 1994) instead draws each zi from its membership probabilities and then draws the parameters given the labels, and produces a sample from the posterior. The widget runs both on flipper length alone.

EM and Gibbs on flipper length

Histogram of the flipper lengths of the 342 penguins, with the current fitted mixture of K normal components (coloured curves) and their sum (thin line). Both algorithms start from the same random means. EM moves deterministically uphill; Gibbs draws labels and parameters at random, so it keeps moving once it has arrived. The lower panel traces the log-likelihood against the iteration number.

With two components, both algorithms quickly find a small-flipper group (Adélie and Chinstrap) and a large-flipper group (Gentoo). Try a few new starts with three components: EM sometimes stops at a poor solution, for instance splitting the Gentoo into two and leaving Adélie and Chinstrap merged, because it only ever climbs. That is a local mode, and the Bayesian posterior has it too, as the next section shows.

11.7 Chains that disagree

We write the mixture in Stan with full covariance matrices for each group (an LKJ prior on each correlation matrix, as in Chapter 6), a Dirichlet(2) prior on the weights, and the per-penguin membership probabilities computed in generated quantities. Each chain starts from a k-means solution.

R
mix_code <- "
data { int<lower=1> N; int<lower=1> D; int<lower=1> K; array[N] vector[D] y; }
parameters {
  simplex[K] w;                                   // group weights
  array[K] vector[D] mu;                          // group means
  array[K] cholesky_factor_corr[D] Omega;         // group correlation matrices
  array[K] vector<lower=0>[D] sigma;              // group standard deviations
}
model {
  array[K] matrix[D, D] Lk;
  w ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(2, K));
  for (k in 1:K) {
    mu[k] ~ normal(0, 1.5); sigma[k] ~ exponential(2); Omega[k] ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
    Lk[k] = diag_pre_multiply(sigma[k], Omega[k]);
  }
  for (n in 1:N) {                                // the group label is summed out
    vector[K] lp;
    for (k in 1:K) lp[k] = log(w[k]) + multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf(y[n] | mu[k], Lk[k]);
    target += log_sum_exp(lp);
  }
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik; array[N] vector[K] prob;     // membership probabilities by Bayes' rule
  { array[K] matrix[D, D] Lk;
    for (k in 1:K) Lk[k] = diag_pre_multiply(sigma[k], Omega[k]);
    for (n in 1:N) { vector[K] lp;
      for (k in 1:K) lp[k] = log(w[k]) + multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf(y[n] | mu[k], Lk[k]);
      log_lik[n] = log_sum_exp(lp); prob[n] = softmax(lp); } }
}"
mix_path <- "fits/ch11_mix_model.rds"                  # cache the compiled model between sessions
if (file.exists(mix_path)) mix_mod <- readRDS(mix_path) else { mix_mod <- stan_model(model_code = mix_code); saveRDS(mix_mod, mix_path) }
fit_mix <- function(Y, K, tag) {
  path <- sprintf("fits/ch11_%s%d.rds", tag, K); if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  set.seed(11); km <- kmeans(Y, K, nstart = 50)            # starting values from k-means
  init <- function() list(w = as.array(as.numeric(table(km$cluster)) / nrow(Y)),
    mu = lapply(1:K, function(k) as.array(km$centers[k, ])),
    sigma = lapply(1:K, function(k) as.array(pmax(apply(Y[km$cluster == k, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd), 0.1))),
    Omega = lapply(1:K, function(k) diag(ncol(Y))))
  fit <- sampling(mix_mod, data = list(N = nrow(Y), D = ncol(Y), K = K, y = lapply(seq_len(nrow(Y)), function(i) Y[i, ])),
                  chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 11, refresh = 0, init = init)
  saveRDS(fit, path); fit
}
m3 <- fit_mix(Yp, 3, "penguin")
c(max_rhat = round(max(summary(m3, pars = c("w", "mu"))$summary[, "Rhat"]), 2), divergences = get_num_divergent(m3))
output
   max_rhat divergences 
      23.48        0.00

The largest R^ is 23.5, although there are no divergent transitions. By every rule used in this course, these chains have not converged.

The diagnostics say the four chains disagree. Before trying to fix anything, look at what each chain found: its average log posterior density, its group weights, and how the penguins it puts in each group line up with the species we hid.

R
per_chain <- function(fit, K) {                  # posterior-mean memberships, one N x K matrix per chain
  arr <- as.array(fit); pn <- grep("^prob\\[", dimnames(arr)[[3]], value = TRUE)
  map(seq_len(dim(arr)[2]), ~ matrix(colMeans(arr[, .x, pn]), ncol = K))
}
lp3 <- colMeans(as.array(m3, pars = "lp__")[, , 1]); P3 <- per_chain(m3, 3)
round(rbind(lp = lp3, sapply(1:4, function(ch) colMeans(as.array(m3, pars = "w")[, ch, ]))), 2)
for (chain in 1:4) { cat("chain", chain, "\n"); print(table(birds$species, group = max.col(P3[[chain]]))) }
output

All four chains reached the same log posterior density (−1210.4 to −1210.9) and put the same penguins together: one group holds 149 Adélie and 4 Chinstrap, another 64 Chinstrap and 2 Adélie, and the third all 123 Gentoo. Only the numbering differs. Gentoo is group 3 in chains 1 and 4, group 2 in chain 2 and group 1 in chain 3. The chains agree completely about the penguins and disagree only about the names.

Two different problems are hiding in that output. The first is label switching. The likelihood is unchanged if we swap the names of two groups: nothing in the data says which group is "1". So a posterior with K well-separated groups has K! identical copies of every mode, one for each labelling, and different chains can land in different copies. Averaging their draws then blends Gentoo with Chinstrap into nonsense, and R^ rightly complains. This is not a problem with the fit, only with its bookkeeping. A common remedy is to constrain one coordinate of the means to be ordered (μ1,1<μ2,1<μ3,1), but it works only if the groups are well separated in that coordinate; Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins have almost the same average bill length, so ordering by bill length would not have helped. The widget shows label switching within a single chain, which happens when groups overlap.

Label switching in a trace plot

A Gibbs sampler for a two-component normal mixture on 100 simulated points, with the true means ±δ/2, both variances 1 and a symmetric prior. The traces show the two component means over 1,500 sweeps. When the components overlap, the sampler swaps their labels from time to time. "Sort" relabels every draw so that component 1 has the smaller mean.

Relabelling fixes the first problem. We take the chain with the highest log posterior as the reference and, for each other chain, choose the permutation of its labels that best matches the reference's membership probabilities (Stephens, 2000, does this draw by draw; chain by chain suffices when labels do not switch within a chain, which the clean per-chain tables above indicate).

The second problem did not occur in this run, but it does in others, and it is not bookkeeping. In an earlier run with a different random seed, one of the four chains settled in a genuinely different solution, a local mode like the one EM gets stuck in: Adélie and Chinstrap merged into one group and a few birds in a small group of their own, with a log posterior density about 50 units below the others. No relabelling turns that into the same answer. Such a mode carries essentially no posterior probability, since e−50 is negligible, but a chain that falls into it cannot climb out. Our align_chains() function therefore keeps only the chains whose average log density is within 10 units of the best, and reports how many it kept. With a minor mode closer in log density, the principled alternative is to weight the chains by their predictive performance (stacking; Yao, Vehtari and Gelman, 2022). We will need the rule for four groups.

R
perms <- function(K) if (K == 1) list(1) else do.call("c", lapply(1:K, function(i) lapply(perms(K - 1), function(p) c(i, ifelse(p >= i, p + 1, p)))))
align_chains <- function(fit, K, gap = 10) {
  lp <- colMeans(as.array(fit, pars = "lp__")[, , 1]); P <- per_chain(fit, K)
  ref <- which.max(lp); keep <- which(lp > max(lp) - gap)            # chains in the dominant mode
  pm <- map(seq_along(P), function(ch) { pp <- perms(K); pp[[which.max(map_dbl(pp, ~ sum(P[[ref]] * P[[ch]][, .x])))]] })
  prob <- Reduce(`+`, map(keep, ~ P[[.x]][, pm[[.x]]])) / length(keep)
  ll <- as.array(fit, pars = "log_lik")[, keep, , drop = FALSE]
  list(prob = prob, keep = keep, lp = lp, loo = suppressWarnings(loo(ll, r_eff = relative_eff(exp(ll)))))
}
a3 <- align_chains(m3, 3)
c(chains_kept = length(a3$keep))
table(birds$species, group = max.col(a3$prob))
c(certain_0.9 = sum(apply(a3$prob, 1, max) > 0.9), uncertain = sum(apply(a3$prob, 1, max) <= 0.9))
output
chains_kept 
          4 
           group
              1   2   3
  Adelie    149   2   0
  Chinstrap   4  64   0
  Gentoo      0   0 123
certain_0.9   uncertain 
        329          13

After relabelling, all four chains are kept and the pooled assignments recover the species almost exactly: 149 of 151 Adélie, 64 of 68 Chinstrap and all 123 Gentoo fall in groups of their own, so only 6 of the 342 penguins are grouped with another species, all of them between Adélie and Chinstrap. 329 penguins are assigned with probability above 0.9; 13 are borderline.

Research Practice: Reporting Latent-Variable Models

  • State the identification strategy: anchors and constraints for a factor model, ordering or relabelling for a mixture. A reader cannot interpret loadings or groups without it.
  • Report every chain, not just the ones that converged. If chains found different modes, say which, how far apart they were in log density, and what you did (relabelled, discarded with a stated rule, or stacked).
  • Report how the number of factors or groups was chosen, with the comparison (LOO or held-out likelihood) and its standard errors, and say where substantive judgement overrode it.
  • For mixtures, report soft assignments: how many cases are confidently assigned and how many are borderline. Downstream analyses that use group labels should carry this uncertainty, for example by repeating the analysis over posterior draws of the labels.
  • When true labels exist for some cases, report agreement with them (a cross-table, or the adjusted Rand index), but do not let a good match be the only justification for the groups.

Check Yourself

Two chains of a three-group mixture have mean log posterior densities of −1212 and −1213 and put the same penguins in the same groups, but under different labels. A third chain has −1262. What is going on?

R-hat is computed on labelled parameters, which label switching scrambles.

More iterations do not help a chain cross a barrier of 50 units of log density.

Label switching changes names, not assignments, so it shows up as chains that agree after a permutation. A genuine local mode puts the penguins in different groups and has a different log density. A gap of about 50 means the mode is about e−50 times less probable, but HMC cannot cross the low-probability valley between modes, so more iterations do not help.

The first two are the same mode with permuted labels (label switching), so relabelling makes them agree. The third is a different, much worse mode with negligible posterior probability that the chain cannot leave; set it aside openly or weight chains by stacking.

11.8 Soft assignments and choosing K

The figure shows every penguin in the two measurements that separate the species best, coloured by its most probable group, with paler points for less certain assignments, and with the hidden species as the marker shape.

R
birds |> mutate(group = factor(max.col(a3$prob)), certainty = apply(a3$prob, 1, max)) |>
  ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, colour = group, shape = species, alpha = certainty)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(harbour[c("sky", "amber", "rose")])) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.25, 1), limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  guides(alpha = "none") + theme(legend.position = "right") +
  labs(x = "bill length (mm)", y = "flipper length (mm)", colour = "group", shape = "species")

The Gentoo group is unmistakable, with its long flippers (and, in the measurements not shown, shallower bills and greater weight). Adélie and Chinstrap differ mainly in bill length, and the pale points, the uncertain assignments, sit where their clouds meet.

R
unc <- order(apply(a3$prob, 1, max))[1:15]
as_tibble(a3$prob[unc, ], .name_repair = ~ paste("group", 1:3)) |>
  mutate(bird = factor(paste0("#", unc, " (", birds$species[unc], ", ", birds$sex[unc], ")"), levels = rev(paste0("#", unc, " (", birds$species[unc], ", ", birds$sex[unc], ")")))) |>
  pivot_longer(-bird, names_to = "group", values_to = "p") |>
  ggplot(aes(p, bird, fill = group)) + geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(harbour[c("sky", "amber", "rose")])) +
  labs(x = "posterior probability", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

The borderline penguins are all on the Adélie–Chinstrap boundary: 11 of the 15 are female Chinstrap and 4 are male Adélie. Small Chinstrap females and large Adélie males overlap in every measurement, so much of the uncertainty is explained by sex, a variable the model never sees. A biologist would recognise these birds as hard cases, and the model says so instead of hiding them in a confident label.

How many groups would the data have chosen without our hint? We fit K=1,…,4 and compare by PSIS-LOO (on one core, the four-group model alone takes about 20 minutes, which is itself a warning sign), using the chains of the dominant mode for each.

R
mk <- map(1:4, ~ fit_mix(Yp, .x, "penguin"))
ak <- map2(mk, 1:4, align_chains)
tibble(K = 1:4, chains_kept = map_int(ak, ~ length(.x$keep)),
       lp_range = map_dbl(ak, ~ round(max(.x$lp) - min(.x$lp), 1)),
       elpd = map_dbl(ak, ~ .x$loo$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"]),
       se = map_dbl(ak, ~ .x$loo$estimates["elpd_loo", "SE"]),
       k_above_0.7 = map_int(ak, ~ sum(.x$loo$diagnostics$pareto_k > 0.7))) |>
  mutate(elpd_vs_3 = elpd - elpd[3], across(c(elpd, se, elpd_vs_3), ~ round(.x, 1)))
table(paste(birds$species, birds$sex), group = max.col(ak[[4]]$prob))
output

The comparison does not stop at three. Two groups are much worse than three (−42.6), but four groups beat three by 121 units of expected log predictive density, about three times the standard errors. That is not the end of the story. With four groups the chains disagreed: their average log densities spanned 70.7 units, only one chain was in the best mode, and so the four-group estimate rests on 500 draws from a single chain, with no guarantee that an even better mode was not missed. Nor is the fourth group a new species, or one sex of a species. Gentoo stays one group; most Chinstrap (with two Adélie males) form another; most Adélie (with six female Chinstrap) a third; and the fourth holds 11 birds, mostly females of the two smaller species. A component like this improves the description of the density by catching birds that sit away from their species' main cloud, but it is not a natural kind. The lesson is the factor model's lesson again: LOO says how many components describe the data best, which is not the same as how many kinds of thing there are.

Choosing K by comparing finite mixtures has a Bayesian alternative: put a prior on partitions with no fixed number of groups. The Dirichlet process (Ferguson, 1973) does this, and its behaviour is easiest to see through the Chinese restaurant process: penguins arrive one at a time; each joins an existing group with probability proportional to its size, or starts a new group with probability proportional to a concentration parameter α. The expected number of groups after n arrivals is ∑i=1nα/(α+i−1), which grows like αlog⁡n. In a Dirichlet process mixture the data then decide how many of these groups are occupied.

The Chinese restaurant process

Left: the prior distribution of the number of groups among n observations under a Dirichlet process with concentration α (2,000 simulations). Right: the group sizes in one simulated seating, largest first.

Two features of the prior matter in practice. Group sizes are very unequal: a few large groups and a tail of small ones, a "rich get richer" pattern that suits some data (species abundances, word frequencies) and not others. And the number of groups keeps growing with n, so a Dirichlet process mixture fitted to a large data set from three true groups tends to report several extra small ones (Miller and Harrison, 2013). That is not a bug in the method, but it means the posterior number of groups is not an estimate of "the" number of clusters; it is the number of components needed to describe the density.

Check Yourself

Under a Chinese restaurant process with α=1, what is the expected number of groups among n=10 observations?

∑i=1nα/(α+i−1)=1+1/2+⋯+1/10.

1+12+13+⋯+110=2.93. For n=340 it is about 6.4, and for n=10,000 about 9.8: logarithmic growth, so the prior always leaves room for one more group.

11.9 Subtypes from expression

The cancer gene-expression project asks the penguin question of tumours: do expression profiles fall into groups, and are they the known molecular subtypes? We return to the TCGA breast-cancer data of Chapter 10 (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Goldman et al., 2020), now taking every primary tumour with a PAM50 subtype call, 844 in all. PAM50 is a 50-gene classifier that assigns each tumour to one of five intrinsic subtypes, Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2-enriched, Basal-like and Normal-like (Parker et al., 2009); the calls play the part of the hidden penguin species. No labels are used in fitting, so there is no training and test split. With 1,000 genes and 844 tumours a full-covariance mixture is out of reach, so we combine this chapter's two tools: reduce the 1,000 most variable genes to their first three principal components, then fit a three-group mixture in that space with the code of Section 11.7.

R
xena <- "https://tcga-xena-hub.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/download/TCGA.BRCA.sampleMap%2F"
dir.create("data/tcga", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
for (f in c("HiSeqV2.gz", "BRCA_clinicalMatrix"))
  if (!file.exists(file.path("data/tcga", f))) download.file(paste0(xena, f), file.path("data/tcga", f))
expr <- read_tsv("data/tcga/HiSeqV2.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
clin <- read_tsv("data/tcga/BRCA_clinicalMatrix", show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 5000)
X <- t(as.matrix(expr[, -1])); colnames(X) <- expr$sample
pam <- clin |> filter(substr(sampleID, 14, 15) == "01", !is.na(PAM50Call_RNAseq))    # primary tumours
X <- X[intersect(rownames(X), pam$sampleID), ]
subtype <- pam$PAM50Call_RNAseq[match(rownames(X), pam$sampleID)]
her2 <- pam$HER2_Final_Status_nature2012[match(rownames(X), pam$sampleID)]
table(subtype)
G <- X[, order(apply(X, 2, var), decreasing = TRUE)[1:1000]]                       # no labels used
pc <- prcomp(G, scale. = TRUE)
round(summary(pc)$importance[2:3, 1:5], 3)
Z <- scale(pc$x[, 1:3])
mt <- fit_mix(Z, 3, "xena"); at <- align_chains(mt, 3)
c(chains_kept = length(at$keep), lp_range = round(max(at$lp) - min(at$lp), 1))
table(subtype, group = max.col(at$prob))
c(uncertain = sum(apply(at$prob, 1, max) <= 0.9))
output

The first three principal components explain 16%, 7% and 4% of the variance in the 1,000 genes, 28% together. The four chains agree after relabelling (log densities within 0.6 of each other). The three groups follow the best-known divisions in breast cancer. Group 1 is Basal-like: it holds 135 of the 141 Basal tumours and nothing else apart from five Normal-like ones. Basal tumours differ from the rest across thousands of genes, so they dominate the first component and separate cleanly, just as the Gentoo penguins did. Group 2 is mostly Luminal A (314 tumours, with 39 Luminal B). Group 3 collects all 67 HER2-enriched tumours and 153 of the 192 Luminal B, but also 107 Luminal A. What separates groups 2 and 3 is roughly the difference between slowly and rapidly dividing tumours, and the PAM50 classes on that axis overlap rather than forming islands. And 279 of the 844 tumours have no group with probability above 0.9: a third of the tumours sit between groups, against 13 of 342 penguins.

R
mt4 <- fit_mix(Z, 4, "xena"); at4 <- align_chains(mt4, 4)
c(chains_kept = length(at4$keep), lp_range = round(max(at4$lp) - min(at4$lp), 1))
loo_compare(list(K3 = at$loo, K4 = at4$loo))
table(subtype, group = max.col(at4$prob))
c(uncertain = sum(apply(at4$prob, 1, max) <= 0.9))
table(clinical_her2 = her2, group_K3 = max.col(at$prob), useNA = "ifany")

PSIS-LOO prefers four groups to three by 25.1 units of expected log predictive density, about three standard errors. The fourth group is mostly HER2-enriched: 41 of its 53 tumours, and 41 of the 67 HER2-enriched tumours overall, with the other 26 joining a group of Luminal B and Luminal A. The Basal group is unchanged, but the extra group buys a better density at the price of more ambiguity: 394 tumours are now uncertain. The last table compares the three groups with clinical HER2 status, the outcome of Chapter 10: group 3 holds 89 of the 113 clinically positive tumours, but they are a minority of it (210 are negative). That is an honest, unglamorous result. HER2 status is decided by the amplification of one small region of chromosome 17, a strong signal in a handful of genes, and a variance-based summary of a thousand genes does not emphasise it; the supervised horseshoe of Chapter 10 found it in one gene. Unsupervised groups are groups in whatever the reduction emphasises.

Check Yourself

A study clusters tumours by expression, finds three groups, and reports that survival differs significantly between them. Which concern is most serious?

Soft assignments are a strength, but they are not the main issue here.

Many good studies use principal components first.

A clustering is a choice among many (features, preprocessing, K, algorithm), and survival differences between groups are easy to find when the choice is made after seeing them. The honest procedure fixes the clustering pipeline in advance or validates the groups and their survival differences in an independent cohort, and propagates membership uncertainty, for example by repeating the survival analysis over posterior draws of the labels.

Unless the number of groups and the clustering were fixed before looking at survival, the analysis may have tried several clusterings and reported the one that separated survival best, and the significance test ignores both that search and the uncertainty in each tumour's group.

Project Connections: Structure Without Labels

For the cancer gene-expression project, Section 10.8 and this section are two halves of one workflow: discover candidate subtypes without labels (factor or principal-component reduction, then a mixture with soft assignments), then ask, with held-out data, whether they predict anything that matters. The TCGA result is the template for an honest report: which known subtypes the groups recover, which they merge, and how many tumours sit between groups. A Bayesian factor model with a horseshoe prior on the loadings (a sparse factor model) is the natural next step for 20,000 genes, because each factor then involves only a few genes and can be read as a pathway. For clustering hostile web traffic, mixtures are the natural model of "kinds of client", and two lessons here transfer directly: run several chains from different starts and report the modes they find, and expect a Dirichlet-process mixture to keep adding small groups as the logs grow, which is useful for spotting new behaviour but makes "the number of attack types" a poorly defined target. For AI-generated text detection, topic models (Chapter 12) are mixtures of words, and the identification and label-switching issues carry over unchanged.

Key Takeaways: Lecture 22

  • A mixture model says each case belongs to one of K latent groups; summing out the label gives a likelihood HMC can sample, and Bayes' rule gives each case a soft assignment.
  • Label switching is bookkeeping: fix it by relabelling chains or draws to a reference. Ordering constraints work only when the groups separate in the ordered coordinate.
  • Local modes are real: chains can settle in different, worse solutions. Compare chains' log posterior densities, report what each found, and set aside or stack them by a stated rule.
  • Choosing K by LOO measures how well the mixture describes the density, which is not the same as counting natural kinds; on the penguins, the data preferred more groups than species.

Lecture 23 — Copulas

11.10 Two genes on one amplicon

Chapter 10 left a puzzle that this lecture takes up. In its Exercise 6 the horseshoe could not decide between ERBB2 and GRB7, two genes a few tens of kilobases apart on chromosome 17 that are amplified together in HER2-positive tumours. Their correlation across tumours is high, but a correlation coefficient is a poor description of how they move together. Look at them across the 1,097 primary tumours of the TCGA data, and at a second pair, ESR1, the gene for the oestrogen receptor, and GATA3, a transcription factor that works with it.

R
library(copula)
xena <- "https://tcga-xena-hub.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/download/TCGA.BRCA.sampleMap%2F"
dir.create("data/tcga", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
if (!file.exists("data/tcga/HiSeqV2.gz")) download.file(paste0(xena, "HiSeqV2.gz"), "data/tcga/HiSeqV2.gz")
expr <- read_tsv("data/tcga/HiSeqV2.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)          # log2(RSEM + 1)
G <- expr |> filter(sample %in% c("ERBB2", "GRB7", "ESR1", "GATA3")) |>
  pivot_longer(-sample, names_to = "tumour") |> pivot_wider(names_from = sample) |>
  filter(substr(tumour, 14, 15) == "01")                                  # primary tumours
nrow(G)
dep <- function(x, y) c(pearson = cor(x, y), spearman = cor(x, y, method = "spearman"),
                        kendall = cor(x, y, method = "kendall"))
rbind(`ERBB2-GRB7, log scale` = dep(G$ERBB2, G$GRB7), `ERBB2-GRB7, raw scale` = dep(2^G$ERBB2, 2^G$GRB7),
      `ESR1-GATA3, log scale` = dep(G$ESR1, G$GATA3), `ESR1-GATA3, raw scale` = dep(2^G$ESR1, 2^G$GATA3)) |> round(3)
output
[1] 1097
                      pearson spearman kendall
ERBB2-GRB7, log scale   0.843    0.678   0.510
ERBB2-GRB7, raw scale   0.871    0.678   0.510
ESR1-GATA3, log scale   0.835    0.717   0.525
ESR1-GATA3, raw scale   0.560    0.717   0.525

The two pairs have almost the same rank correlations: Kendall's τ is 0.510 for ERBB2 and GRB7 and 0.525 for ESR1 and GATA3, and Spearman's 0.678 and 0.717. Pearson's correlation is higher, 0.843 and 0.835, on the log scale on which expression is usually analysed; on the original scale of normalised counts it is 0.871 for the first pair but only 0.560 for the second. The rank correlations do not change at all. A dependence measure that changes when the data are re-expressed is describing the margins as much as the dependence.

R
pobs <- function(x) rank(x) / (length(x) + 1)                 # pseudo-observations
pairs_long <- bind_rows(
  tibble(pair = "ERBB2 and GRB7", x = G$ERBB2, y = G$GRB7),
  tibble(pair = "ESR1 and GATA3", x = G$ESR1, y = G$GATA3)) |>
  mutate(u = pobs(x), v = pobs(y), .by = pair)
p_log <- ggplot(pairs_long, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.45, colour = harbour[["sky"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ pair, ncol = 1, scales = "free") + labs(x = "first gene, log2 expression", y = "second gene")
p_rank <- ggplot(pairs_long, aes(u, v)) + geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.45, colour = harbour[["sky"]]) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.95, xmax = 1, ymin = 0.95, ymax = 1, fill = NA, colour = harbour[["rose"]], linetype = 2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 0.05, ymin = 0, ymax = 0.05, fill = NA, colour = harbour[["rose"]], linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ pair, ncol = 1) + coord_equal() + labs(x = "rank of first gene", y = "rank of second gene")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_log, p_rank, widths = c(1.15, 1))

The two pairs have almost the same rank correlation, yet they are dependent in opposite ways. For ERBB2 and GRB7 the dependence is loose among ordinary tumours and very tight at the top: when the amplicon is amplified, both genes are pushed to extreme values together. For ESR1 and GATA3 it is the other way round: tumours that have lost the oestrogen-receptor programme, mostly the Basal tumours of Section 11.9, have both genes very low, while among the oestrogen-receptor-positive majority the two vary fairly independently. A correlation coefficient, or a bivariate normal distribution, cannot tell these two pictures apart. The tool that can is the copula: the joint distribution of the ranks, stripped of the margins.

11.11 Sklar's theorem

The construction rests on one simple fact, the probability integral transform: if X is continuous with distribution function F, then U=F(X) is uniform on (0,1), because Pr(F(X)≤u)=Pr(X≤F−1(u))=u. Run backwards, it is how a computer simulates from any distribution: draw U uniform and return F−1(U). Apply it to each coordinate of a pair (X,Y) with margins F and G, and the pair (U,V)=(F(X),G(Y)) has uniform margins. Its joint distribution function

C(u,v)=Pr(U≤u,V≤v),0≤u,v≤1,

is a copula: a bivariate distribution function on the unit square with uniform margins. Everything about how X and Y depend on each other is in C, and nothing about their individual distributions is.

Result: Sklar's Theorem (Sklar, 1959)

Let H be a joint distribution function with margins F and G. Then there is a copula C such that

H(x,y)=C(F(x),G(y))for all x,y.

If F and G are continuous, C is unique. Conversely, for any copula C and any distribution functions F and G, the formula defines a joint distribution function with margins F and G.

We prove the continuous case. Let U=F(X) and V=G(Y). For continuous F, Pr(U≤u)=Pr(X≤F−1(u))=F(F−1(u))=u, where F−1(u)=inf{x:F(x)≥u}, so U is uniform, and likewise V. Let C be the joint distribution function of (U,V), a copula. Since F is non-decreasing, X≤x implies F(X)≤F(x), and F(X)≤F(x) implies X≤x except on an event of probability zero, so

H(x,y)=Pr(X≤x,Y≤y)=Pr(U≤F(x),V≤G(y))=C(F(x),G(y)).

Uniqueness: every u∈(0,1) is F(x) for some x when F is continuous, so C(u,v)=H(F−1(u),G−1(v)) is determined by H everywhere. For the converse, let (U,V) have distribution function C and set X=F−1(U), Y=G−1(V). Because F−1(u)≤x exactly when u≤F(x), Pr(X≤x,Y≤y)=Pr(U≤F(x),V≤G(y))=C(F(x),G(y)), and setting y=∞ shows that X has margin F. ∎

The converse is also how copula models are simulated: draw (U,V) from C, then transform each coordinate with the inverse distribution function of the margin you want. Differentiating H gives the density,

h(x,y)=c(F(x),G(y))f(x)g(y),c(u,v)=∂2C(u,v)∂u∂v,

so the log-likelihood of n pairs splits into three parts, one for each margin and one for the dependence:

log⁡L=∑i=1nlog⁡f(xi)+∑i=1nlog⁡g(yi)+∑i=1nlog⁡c(F(xi),G(yi)).

This is what makes copulas useful in applied work. The margins can be anything: a gamma for waiting times, a Poisson for goals, a mixture for a bimodal gene, or no model at all. The dependence is then modelled separately, with a family chosen for the shape of the dependence rather than forced on it by the margins. A bivariate normal distribution is the special case of normal margins with a Gaussian copula; change either part and you have a model the bivariate normal cannot express.

Four consequences follow directly.

  • Invariance. If α and β are strictly increasing, (α(X),β(Y)) has the same copula as (X,Y), because the ranks do not change. So any measure of dependence that depends only on the copula is unchanged by taking logarithms, square roots or any other monotone transformation. Pearson's correlation is not such a measure; the output in Section 11.10 shows it falling from 0.835 to 0.560 when the expression of ESR1 and GATA3 is taken off the log scale, while both rank correlations stay exactly the same.
  • Rank correlations are copula properties. Kendall's τ, the probability that two tumours are ranked the same way on both genes minus the probability that they are ranked the opposite way, and Spearman's ρS, the correlation of the ranks, are
τ=4∫01∫01C(u,v)dC(u,v)−1,ρS=12∫01∫01C(u,v)dudv−3.
  • Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds. Every copula lies between two extremes:
max(u+v−1,0)≤C(u,v)≤min(u,v).

The upper bound is perfect positive dependence (V=U), the lower bound perfect negative dependence (V=1−U), and independence is the product copula Π(u,v)=uv. A consequence that surprises people: for given margins, not every Pearson correlation between −1 and 1 is attainable. Two lognormal variables with very different variances cannot have correlation 1 even when one is an increasing function of the other, which is one reason a correlation matrix is a poor specification of a joint distribution (Embrechts, McNeil and Straumann, 2002).

  • Tail dependence. The upper and lower tail dependence coefficients,
λU=limq→1Pr(V>q∣U>q),λL=limq→0Pr(V≤q∣U≤q),

measure whether extremes happen together. If λU=0.6, then given that one variable is beyond a very high quantile, the other is beyond it too with probability about 0.6, however extreme the quantile. If λU=0, joint extremes become rarer than single ones as the threshold rises, even when the variables are strongly correlated.

11.12 A small zoo of copulas

Five families cover most applied work. Each has one parameter, and each is most easily understood through the Kendall's τ it implies, which lets families be compared at the same overall strength of dependence.

FamilyC(u,v)Kendall's τ(λL,λU)
Gaussian, −1<ρ<1Φρ(Φ−1(u),Φ−1(v))2πarcsinρ(0,0)
Student t, −1<ρ<1, ν>0tρ,ν(tν−1(u),tν−1(v))2πarcsinρ(λt,λt)
Clayton, θ>0(u−θ+v−θ−1)−1/θθ/(θ+2)(2−1/θ,0)
Gumbel, θ≥1exp⁡(−[u~θ+v~θ]1/θ)1−1/θ(0,2−21/θ)
Frank, θ≠0−1θlog⁡(1+(e−θu−1)(e−θv−1)e−θ−1)1−4θ(1−D1(θ))(0,0)

Here u~=−log⁡u and v~=−log⁡v in the Gumbel copula, Φρ is the standard bivariate normal distribution function with correlation ρ, tρ,ν its Student-t analogue, λt=2tν+1(−(ν+1)(1−ρ)/(1+ρ)), and D1(θ)=θ−1∫0θs/(es−1)ds is the Debye function. The Gaussian and Frank copulas have no tail dependence; the t has the same amount in both tails, shrinking as ν grows; Clayton has it only in the lower tail and Gumbel only in the upper. Any copula can be rotated: the survival copula, the copula of (1−U,1−V), swaps the tails, so a survival Gumbel has lower tail dependence and a survival Clayton upper. Clayton and Gumbel belong to the Archimedean class, C(u,v)=ψ(ψ−1(u)+ψ−1(v)) for a decreasing generator ψ, which is also how they are simulated: Gumbel's generator is the Laplace transform of a positive stable variable, Clayton's that of a gamma variable, so both are a shared random "frailty" that pushes the two variables up or down together.

Same correlation, different tails

1,000 draws from a copula with the chosen family and Kendall's τ. Left: the copula itself, on the unit square. Right: the same draws with standard normal margins, (Φ−1(U),Φ−1(V)), which stretches the corners so that the tails can be seen; for the Gaussian copula this is an ordinary bivariate normal sample. The dashed squares are the top and bottom 5% of both variables. Every family at a given τ has the same rank correlation, but not the same corners.

Set τ=0.5 and step through the families. The Gaussian and Frank clouds are symmetric and thin out in both corners; Frank is the more evenly spread. Clayton pinches into a point at the lower left and fans out at the upper right; Gumbel does the opposite. On the unit square the differences look modest, because the corners are small. On the normal scale they are obvious: under Clayton the lower-left tail is a tight streak, under the Gaussian copula an ellipse. The readout counts the draws in the two corner squares. Under independence each would hold 0.25% of the draws; at τ=0.5 the Gaussian copula puts about 2.0% in each and Frank 1.1%, while Gumbel puts 3.0% in the upper square and Clayton 3.5% in the lower one. For anything that depends on joint extremes, such as two hospitals both overwhelmed on the same day or two assets both crashing, those factors of two or three are the whole story.

Check Yourself

A pair of variables has a Gaussian copula with ρ=0.5. What is Kendall's τ? (What is it if the margins are changed to exponential?)

Use τ=2πarcsinρ, and remember that τ depends on the copula only.

τ=2πarcsin(0.5)=2π·π6=13≈0.333, whatever the margins: exponential, lognormal or anything else, because changing the margins applies an increasing transformation to each variable and leaves the ranks, and hence the copula, unchanged. Pearson's correlation would change with the margins.

11.13 Fitting copulas in Stan

Bayesian inference for a copula follows from the split likelihood of Section 11.11. The full approach models the margins and the copula together and samples everything jointly; it is the right choice when the margins are of interest, or when the data are discrete (Section 11.15). When the margins are awkward and the question is about dependence, as with these genes, a common shortcut replaces F(xi) and G(yi) by the scaled ranks ui=rank(xi)/(n+1) and vi=rank(yi)/(n+1), the pseudo-observations plotted in Section 11.10, and treats ∑ilog⁡c(ui,vi) as the likelihood of the copula parameter (Genest, Ghoudi and Rivest, 1995). The ranks are not quite independent data, so this is a pseudo-likelihood and its posterior is slightly too narrow; with a thousand tumours and one parameter the effect is small, and Section 11.14 shows the fully Bayesian alternative.

One Stan program fits all five candidate copulas. We write each density in terms of its log, put the same uniform prior on Kendall's τ for every family, and convert τ to the family's own parameter with the formulas in the table, so that the families are compared on equal terms. The survival versions are obtained by flipping the data, (1−u,1−v).

R
cop_code <- "
functions {
  vector cop_lpdf_vec(vector a, vector b, vector x, vector y, real theta, int family) {
    if (family == 1)                                                  // Gaussian
      return -0.5 * log1m(theta^2) - (theta^2 * (x .* x + y .* y) - 2 * theta * x .* y) / (2 * (1 - theta^2));
    if (family == 2 || family == 4) {                                 // Gumbel
      vector[rows(a)] s = x .^ theta + y .^ theta;
      vector[rows(a)] A = s .^ (1 / theta);
      return -A - log(a) - log(b) + (theta - 1) * (log(x) + log(y)) + (1 / theta - 2) * log(s) + log(A + theta - 1);
    }
    return log1p(theta) - (1 + theta) * (log(a) + log(b))             // Clayton
           - (2 + 1 / theta) * log(a .^ (-theta) + b .^ (-theta) - 1);
  }
}
data {
  int<lower=1> N; vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] u; vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] v;
  int<lower=1, upper=5> family;      // 1 Gaussian, 2 Gumbel, 3 Clayton, 4 survival Gumbel, 5 survival Clayton
}
transformed data {
  vector[N] a = family >= 4 ? 1 - u : u;               // a survival copula is the copula of (1 - U, 1 - V)
  vector[N] b = family >= 4 ? 1 - v : v;
  vector[N] x = family == 1 ? inv_Phi(a) : -log(a);
  vector[N] y = family == 1 ? inv_Phi(b) : -log(b);
}
parameters { real<lower=0, upper=0.95> tau; }         // Kendall's tau, uniform prior for every family
transformed parameters {
  real theta = family == 1 ? sin(pi() * tau / 2)
             : (family == 2 || family == 4) ? 1 / (1 - tau) : 2 * tau / (1 - tau);
}
model { target += sum(cop_lpdf_vec(a, b, x, y, theta, family)); }
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik = cop_lpdf_vec(a, b, x, y, theta, family);
  real lambda = family == 1 ? 0 : (family == 2 || family == 4) ? 2 - 2^(1 / theta) : 2^(-1 / theta);
}"
cop_path <- "fits/ch11_cop_model.rds"
if (file.exists(cop_path)) cop_mod <- readRDS(cop_path) else { cop_mod <- stan_model(model_code = cop_code); saveRDS(cop_mod, cop_path) }
families <- c(Gaussian = 1, Gumbel = 2, Clayton = 3, `survival Gumbel` = 4, `survival Clayton` = 5)
fit_cop <- function(x, y, tag) map(families, function(f) {
  path <- sprintf("fits/ch11_cop_%s_%d.rds", tag, f); if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  fit <- sampling(cop_mod, data = list(N = length(x), u = pobs(x), v = pobs(y), family = f),
                  chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 11, refresh = 0)
  saveRDS(fit, path); fit })
compare_cop <- function(fits) {
  loos <- map(fits, function(f) { ll <- extract_log_lik(f, merge_chains = FALSE); loo(ll, r_eff = relative_eff(exp(ll))) })
  cmp <- loo_compare(loos)
  tibble(family = rownames(cmp), elpd_diff = cmp[, "elpd_diff"], se_diff = cmp[, "se_diff"]) |>
    left_join(map_dfr(fits, function(f) { s <- summary(f, pars = c("tau", "lambda"))$summary
      tibble(tau = s["tau", "mean"], lambda = s["lambda", "mean"], rhat = s["tau", "Rhat"]) }, .id = "family"), by = "family") |>
    mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 3)))
}
fits_her2 <- fit_cop(G$ERBB2, G$GRB7, "her2"); fits_er <- fit_cop(G$ESR1, G$GATA3, "er")
compare_cop(fits_her2)
compare_cop(fits_er)
output

1 Gumbel               0        0    0.546  0.63   1.00
2 survival Clayton    -0.009    8.55 0.517  0.724  1.00
3 Gaussian           -87.5     10.5  0.519  0      1.00
4 survival Gumbel   -150.      13.6  0.475  0.561  1.00
5 Clayton           -253.      20.0  0.367  0.55   1.01
# A tibble: 5 x 6
  family           elpd_diff se_diff   tau lambda  rhat
  <chr>                <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 Clayton              0        0    0.475  0.682  1.00
2 survival Gumbel     -0.549    8.93 0.51   0.596  1.00
3 Gaussian           -50.6     18.5  0.499  0      1.01
4 Gumbel            -159.      22.2  0.432  0.517  1.01
5 survival Clayton  -253.      22.8  0.311  0.464  1.00

The two pairs give mirror-image answers. For ERBB2 and GRB7, the two families with upper tail dependence only, Gumbel and survival Clayton, are indistinguishable (difference 0.0, standard error 8.6) and beat the Gaussian copula by 87.5 units of expected log predictive density, more than eight standard errors; the families with lower tail dependence are far worse. For ESR1 and GATA3 the order is reversed: Clayton and survival Gumbel lead and beat the Gaussian by 50.6 (standard error 18.5), and the upper-tail families come last. All chains converged (R^≤1.01). The posterior means of τ are close to the sample values but not equal to them (0.546 for Gumbel against 0.510; 0.475 for Clayton against 0.525), because each family's τ is the value at which that family best matches the whole shape of the copula; a family of the wrong shape distorts it badly (Clayton gives 0.367 for the first pair). The winners' tail dependence, λU=0.63 for Gumbel and λL=0.68 for Clayton, says that given one gene is extreme, the other is too about two times in three.

The question that matters in practice is how much the choice changes a prediction about extremes. Take the probability that a tumour is in the top 5% for both ERBB2 and GRB7: under independence it would be 0.052=0.0025, and with perfect dependence 0.05. For ESR1 and GATA3 the corresponding question is about the bottom 5%. Each copula answers it through Pr(U>q,V>q)=1−2q+C(q,q), which we compute for every posterior draw.

R
joint_tail <- function(fit, f, q, upper) {        # posterior draws of Pr(both beyond the q-quantile)
  th <- rstan::extract(fit, "theta")$theta[seq(1, 2000, by = 4)]
  rot <- f >= 4; lowr <- if (upper) !rot else rot  # which corner of the fitted (possibly rotated) copula
  Cqq <- function(t, p) switch(as.character(f), `1` = pCopula(c(p, p), normalCopula(t)),
    `2` = , `4` = p^(2^(1 / t)), `3` = , `5` = (2 * p^(-t) - 1)^(-1 / t))
  map_dbl(th, function(t) if (lowr) 1 - 2 * q + Cqq(t, q) else Cqq(t, 1 - q))
}
tail_table <- function(fits, x, y, upper) map_dfr(c(0.95, 0.99), function(p) {
  emp <- if (upper) mean(pobs(x) > p & pobs(y) > p) else mean(pobs(x) < 1 - p & pobs(y) < 1 - p)
  bind_rows(tibble(model = "observed", mean = emp, lo = NA, hi = NA),
            imap_dfr(fits, function(f, nm) { d <- joint_tail(f, families[[nm]], p, upper)
              tibble(model = nm, mean = mean(d), lo = quantile(d, 0.05), hi = quantile(d, 0.95)) })) |>
    mutate(quantile = p, .before = 1) }) |> mutate(across(c(mean, lo, hi), ~ round(.x, 4)))
tail_table(fits_her2[c("Gaussian", "Gumbel")], G$ERBB2, G$GRB7, upper = TRUE)
tail_table(fits_er[c("Gaussian", "Clayton")], G$ESR1, G$GATA3, upper = FALSE)
# conditional exceedance curves for the widget below, at the posterior mean of each copula
Cdiag <- function(f, t, p) switch(as.character(f), `1` = pCopula(c(p, p), normalCopula(t)), `2` = p^(2^(1 / t)),
  `3` = (2 * p^(-t) - 1)^(-1 / t), `4` = 2 * p - 1 + (1 - p)^(2^(1 / t)), `5` = 2 * p - 1 + (2 * (1 - p)^(-t) - 1)^(-1 / t))
qs <- seq(0.5, 0.99, by = 0.01)
curves <- function(fits, x, y) { u <- pobs(x); v <- pobs(y)
  list(emp_upper = round(map_dbl(qs, ~ mean(u > .x & v > .x) / mean(u > .x)), 4),
       emp_lower = round(map_dbl(qs, ~ mean(u < 1 - .x & v < 1 - .x) / mean(u < 1 - .x)), 4),
       model = imap(fits, function(f, nm) { t <- mean(rstan::extract(f, "theta")$theta); fam <- families[[nm]]
         list(upper = round(map_dbl(qs, ~ (1 - 2 * .x + Cdiag(fam, t, .x)) / (1 - .x)), 4),
              lower = round(map_dbl(qs, ~ Cdiag(fam, t, 1 - .x) / (1 - .x)), 4)) })) }
writeLines(paste0("var C11C=", jsonlite::toJSON(list(q = qs, her2 = curves(fits_her2, G$ERBB2, G$GRB7),
  er = curves(fits_er, G$ESR1, G$GATA3)), auto_unbox = TRUE), ";"), "data/ch11_cop.js")
