1     0.95 observed 0.0201 NA      NA     
2     0.95 Gaussian 0.0199  0.0189  0.0208
3     0.95 Clayton  0.0342  0.0332  0.035 
4     0.99 observed 0.0018 NA      NA     
5     0.99 Gaussian 0.0027  0.0025  0.0029
6     0.99 Clayton  0.0068  0.0066  0.007

At the 95th percentile, the Gumbel copula is much closer to the data than the Gaussian for ERBB2 and GRB7: it predicts 3.2% of tumours in the top corner (90% interval 3.1% to 3.3%), the Gaussian 2.1%, and 3.9% (43 tumours) are observed. At the 99th percentile the picture flips: 3 tumours (0.27%) are in the corner, which is what the Gaussian predicts (0.29%), while the Gumbel predicts 0.63%. For ESR1 and GATA3 the Gaussian matches the observed share in the bottom 5% (2.0%) and Clayton, the LOO winner, overpredicts it (3.4%). Two lessons follow. First, these intervals are far too narrow to believe: they describe uncertainty about τ within one family, with ranks treated as data, not uncertainty about the shape of the tail, and the top 1% of each gene contains only 11 tumours. Second, the family that fits best overall need not fit best in every corner.

R
set.seed(11); n <- nrow(G)
tau_post <- function(f) mean(rstan::extract(f, "tau")$tau)
sims <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = "observed", u = pobs(G$ERBB2), v = pobs(G$GRB7)),
  as_tibble(rCopula(n, normalCopula(sin(pi * tau_post(fits_her2$Gaussian) / 2))), .name_repair = ~ c("u", "v")) |> mutate(panel = "Gaussian copula"),
  as_tibble(rCopula(n, gumbelCopula(1 / (1 - tau_post(fits_her2$Gumbel)))), .name_repair = ~ c("u", "v")) |> mutate(panel = "Gumbel copula")) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, c("observed", "Gaussian copula", "Gumbel copula")))
ggplot(filter(sims, u > 0.8, v > 0.8), aes(u, v)) + geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.6, colour = harbour[["sky"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0.8, 1), ylim = c(0.8, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.8, 0.9, 1)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.8, 0.9, 1)) +
  labs(x = "rank of ERBB2", y = "rank of GRB7")

The widget sets the fitted copulas side by side through the quantity that defines tail dependence, Pr(V>q∣U>q), as q moves toward 1 (or Pr(V≤q∣U≤q) as q moves toward 0).

Do extremes come together?

The conditional probability that the second gene is beyond a quantile, given that the first is, for the observed tumours (points) and for each fitted copula at its posterior mean (lines). The horizontal axis is how far into the tail the threshold sits: 0.5 is the median, 0.99 the most extreme 1%. Independence gives the dotted line, 1−q.

Look at the points rather than the lines. For ERBB2 and GRB7 in the upper tail, the observed conditional probability rises to 0.94 at q=0.9 and then falls, to 0.80 at 0.95 and 0.57 at 0.98. For ESR1 and GATA3 in the lower tail it peaks at about 0.9 near q=0.75, the bottom quarter, and falls to 0.29 at 0.98. No one-parameter family has this shape: the Gaussian curve falls steadily toward zero, while Gumbel and Clayton level off at their λ. The shape is that of a mixture. About one tumour in seven is HER2-positive (Section 10.8), and in those tumours both genes are pushed above everyone else's, so a tumour in the top 10% for ERBB2 is almost always in the top 10% for GRB7; within the amplified tumours the two genes are still strongly related but not in lockstep, so once the threshold lies deep inside the amplified group, the conditional probability falls. In the same way, about 23% of the tumours are oestrogen-receptor negative and have both ESR1 and GATA3 low. The copula of these data is a mixture of copulas, one for each kind of tumour, and the model it calls for is a Lecture 22 mixture with a copula inside each component (Exercise 11). The one-parameter families were still informative: LOO picked the right tail for each pair, and Gumbel beat the Gaussian around the 90th to 95th percentiles where the amplified tumours sit. But a tail dependence coefficient is a limit that finite data never reach, so report joint exceedance probabilities at thresholds the data can support, and check them against the data.

Warning: The Formula That Was Blamed

In 2000 David Li proposed modelling the times to default of many companies with a Gaussian copula, with a single correlation parameter calibrated from market prices (Li, 2000). The model made it easy to price collateralised debt obligations, and it became an industry standard. When US house prices fell in 2007 and 2008, defaults arrived together on a scale the models had treated as almost impossible, and the Gaussian copula was blamed in the press as "the formula that killed Wall Street". The history is more complicated: practitioners knew the model's limits and used it as a pricing convention as much as a description of risk (MacKenzie and Spears, 2014). But the statistical point is exactly the one above. A Gaussian copula has no tail dependence, so it says that joint extremes become negligible as they become more extreme, and a single correlation fitted to ordinary times says nothing about whether that is true. Whenever a conclusion depends on joint extremes, the copula family must be checked against the tails of the data, and when the tails are thin in the data, the uncertainty about them must be reported.

Check Yourself

Two analysts fit copulas to daily rainfall at two weather stations. One fits a Gaussian copula, the other a Gumbel copula, and both find Kendall's τ=0.4. Which statement is right?

Kendall's tau summarises the whole copula, not its tails.

Copulas are defined for any continuous margins.

Copula families with the same τ can differ greatly in the corners. With θ=5/3, 21/θ=20.6≈1.516, so λU≈0.48: given that one station has an extreme day, the other does too about half the time, however extreme the threshold. The Gaussian copula says that this conditional probability falls to zero. For flood risk, which depends on several catchments flooding together, the choice dominates the answer.

The models agree on the rank correlation but not on joint extremes: the Gumbel copula has upper tail dependence λU=2−21/θ with θ=1/(1−τ)≈1.67, so about 0.48, and gives a much higher probability of a joint extreme than the Gaussian, for which λU=0. The data's upper corner, and a comparison such as LOO, should decide.

11.14 Mixed data and the Gaussian copula

The questionnaire of Lecture 21 is the opposite problem: the items are coded 1 to 6, so their margins are discrete, and the factor model treated the codes as if they were continuous and normal. Discrete margins break the neat story of Section 11.11. The probability integral transform F(X) of a discrete variable is not uniform, and Sklar's copula is no longer unique: many copulas give the same joint distribution of the codes, and rank-based estimates are biased by the ties (Genest and Nešlehová, 2007).

The Gaussian copula has a way through, because it is a latent-variable model. Suppose each person has a latent vector zi∼normal(0,R), with R a correlation matrix, and each observed variable is an increasing function of one coordinate, yij=Fj−1(Φ(zij)). For a continuous variable that is the Gaussian copula with margin Fj. For an ordinal item it is the threshold model of Chapter 4, with yij=k when zij falls between two cut points. Peter Hoff (2007) noticed that one does not need to model the margins at all. Whatever the increasing functions are, the observed data tell us the order of the latent values within each variable: if person i gave a higher code than person i′ on item j, then zij>zi′j, and ties say nothing. The probability that the latent normal vectors respect all these orderings depends only on R. This extended rank likelihood gives a posterior for R that is the same whichever increasing functions produced the data, and a Gibbs sampler that draws each zij from a truncated normal between its neighbours in the ordering. It handles continuous, ordinal and binary variables together, and missing values are simply left unconstrained, so they are imputed as part of the sampler (Chapter 7). The sbgcop package implements it.

We apply it to the five Neuroticism items, which ask how easily people get angry, irritated, moody, blue and panicky, together with three variables of different kinds: education (an ordinal code from 1 to 5, missing for 223 people), age (continuous and skewed) and a female indicator (binary).

R
tmp <- tempfile()
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cran/psychTools/master/data/bfi.rda", tmp, quiet = TRUE)
load(tmp)
D <- bfi |> transmute(N1, N2, N3, N4, N5, education, age, female = as.integer(gender == 2)) |> as.matrix()
c(people = nrow(D), missing = sum(is.na(D)))
set.seed(11)
gc_path <- "fits/ch11_sbgcop.rds"
if (file.exists(gc_path)) gc_fit <- readRDS(gc_path) else {
  gc_fit <- sbgcop::sbgcop.mcmc(D, nsamp = 2000, odens = 4, verb = FALSE); saveRDS(gc_fit, gc_path) }
R_draws <- gc_fit$C.psamp                                    # 8 x 8 x 500 posterior draws of R
R_mean <- apply(R_draws, c(1, 2), mean)
round(R_mean, 2)
output

N2         0.77  1.00  0.60  0.43  0.39     -0.06 -0.10   0.13

N4         0.44  0.43  0.57  1.00  0.44      0.01 -0.04   0.01

R
pr <- which(upper.tri(R_mean), arr.ind = TRUE)
P <- cor(D, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cmp <- tibble(pair = paste(colnames(D)[pr[, 1]], "and", colnames(D)[pr[, 2]]), copula = R_mean[pr],
              lo = apply(R_draws, 3, function(m) m[pr]) |> apply(1, quantile, 0.05),
              hi = apply(R_draws, 3, function(m) m[pr]) |> apply(1, quantile, 0.95), pearson = P[pr]) |>
  filter(abs(copula) > 0.08) |> mutate(pair = fct_reorder(pair, copula))
ggplot(cmp, aes(y = pair)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = harbour[["grid"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(x = pearson), colour = harbour[["sky"]], size = 1.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = harbour[["rose"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(x = copula), colour = harbour[["rose"]], size = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "correlation (blue: Pearson on codes; red: Gaussian copula, 90% interval)", y = NULL)

Almost every latent correlation in the figure is further from zero than Pearson's correlation of the codes; the exceptions are the small correlations with age, where the two agree. For pairs of items the difference is modest (N1 and N2: 0.77, 90% interval 0.75 to 0.78, against 0.71), because six-point items keep most of the information. It is largest where a variable is coarse: education and age correlate 0.35 (0.32 to 0.39) on the latent scale against 0.24 for Pearson, and the binary female indicator correlates 0.29 (0.25 to 0.33) with N5, panicking easily, against 0.21. Pearson's correlation of codes is attenuated: coding throws away information that the latent values had. The copula estimates the correlation of the underlying continuous quantities, under the assumption that they are jointly normal after some increasing transformation of each, which the data cannot check for a binary variable and can only partly check for an ordinal one. The 342 missing values, 223 of them for education, were imputed inside the sampler, so nobody was dropped, and age, which is strongly skewed in this sample, needed no transformation, because the rank likelihood uses only its ordering.

The latent correlation matrix is a natural input to the factor model of Section 11.4: instead of treating codes as normal, put the factor structure on R, so that zi=Λfi+εi on the latent scale. This is the Gaussian copula factor model of Murray et al. (2013), which keeps the interpretation of Lecture 21 while respecting the ordinal nature of the items, and lets binary, count and continuous variables load on the same factors.

Check Yourself

Why can't the pseudo-observations of Section 11.13 simply be computed from the questionnaire codes and fed to the Stan program?

Ranks can be computed for any variable that can be ordered.

The Gaussian copula is used for these data in this very section.

Sklar's theorem guarantees a unique copula only for continuous margins. With discrete margins, F(X) takes a few values, not a uniform spread, and many copulas reproduce the same table of codes. Treating ties as data attenuates the dependence, which is what the Pearson correlations in Section 11.14 show; the extended rank likelihood (or a full model of discrete margins, as in Section 11.15) avoids it.

With six possible codes and 2,800 people, almost every rank is tied, so the scaled ranks are far from uniform and the copula of the codes is not unique. The rank-based pseudo-likelihood treats the tied values as if they were the latent values, which biases the dependence toward zero; the extended rank likelihood uses only the orderings the codes actually reveal.

11.15 Copulas in applied projects

The three uses above, describing tail dependence, separating margins from dependence, and modelling mixed data on a latent scale, are the common ones in applied work. A fourth is a check of an assumption that most models make silently: that two outcomes are independent given the model's predictors. The football model of the Afterword, like most models of match results, gives home and away goals independent Poisson distributions given the two teams' strengths. In the Premier League the two scores are negatively correlated, which suggests the assumption is wrong. But the correlation of the raw scores mixes two things: dependence within a match, and the fact that a strong team both scores more and concedes less. A copula on the conditional margins separates them.

Goals are counts, so we use the full likelihood rather than ranks. For a match with home goals x and away goals y, Poisson margins F and G given the team strengths, and a copula C, the probability of the score is the probability of a rectangle,

Pr(X=x,Y=y)=C(F(x),G(y))−C(F(x−1),G(y))−C(F(x),G(y−1))+C(F(x−1),G(y−1)),

which is how any copula is applied to discrete margins. We use the Frank copula, which allows negative as well as positive dependence and has no tail dependence to confuse with the small counts, and fit it jointly with the attack and defence strengths of every team in each of six seasons (2019/20 to 2024/25, 2,280 matches), using the data of the Afterword.

R
seasons <- c("1920", "2021", "2122", "2223", "2324", "2425")
for (s in seasons) { f <- sprintf("data/football/E0_%s.csv", s)
  if (!file.exists(f)) download.file(sprintf("https://www.football-data.co.uk/mmz4281/%s/E0.csv", s), f) }
epl <- map_dfr(seasons, function(s) read_csv(sprintf("data/football/E0_%s.csv", s), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(season = s, home = HomeTeam, away = AwayTeam, hg = FTHG, ag = FTAG))
teams <- sort(unique(c(paste(epl$season, epl$home), paste(epl$season, epl$away))))
c(matches = nrow(epl), team_seasons = length(teams), raw_correlation = round(cor(epl$hg, epl$ag), 3))
foot_code <- "
functions {
  real frank_C(real u, real v, real theta) {          // Frank copula C(u, v)
    if (u <= 0 || v <= 0) return 0;
    return -log1p(expm1(-theta * u) * expm1(-theta * v) / expm1(-theta)) / theta;
  }
  real rect(real F1, real F0, real G1, real G0, real theta) {
    return frank_C(F1, G1, theta) - frank_C(F0, G1, theta) - frank_C(F1, G0, theta) + frank_C(F0, G0, theta);
  }
}
data { int<lower=1> N; int<lower=1> T; array[N] int<lower=0> hg; array[N] int<lower=0> ag;
       array[N] int<lower=1, upper=T> ht; array[N] int<lower=1, upper=T> at; }
parameters { real mu; real home; vector[T] att_z; vector[T] def_z; real<lower=0> s_att; real<lower=0> s_def; real theta; }
transformed parameters { vector[T] att = s_att * att_z; vector[T] def = s_def * def_z; }
model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 1); home ~ normal(0, 0.5); att_z ~ std_normal(); def_z ~ std_normal();
  s_att ~ normal(0, 0.5); s_def ~ normal(0, 0.5); theta ~ normal(0, 3);
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real lh = exp(mu + home + att[ht[n]] - def[at[n]]);  real la = exp(mu + att[at[n]] - def[ht[n]]);
    target += log(rect(poisson_cdf(hg[n] | lh), hg[n] > 0 ? poisson_cdf(hg[n] - 1 | lh) : 0,
                       poisson_cdf(ag[n] | la), ag[n] > 0 ? poisson_cdf(ag[n] - 1 | la) : 0, theta));
  }
}
generated quantities {                                 // predicted share of draws, 0-0 and 1-1, with and without the copula
  real p_draw = 0; real p_draw_ind = 0; real p00 = 0; real p00_ind = 0; real p11 = 0; real p11_ind = 0;
  vector[N] lam_h; vector[N] lam_a;
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real lh = exp(mu + home + att[ht[n]] - def[at[n]]);  real la = exp(mu + att[at[n]] - def[ht[n]]);
    lam_h[n] = lh; lam_a[n] = la;
    for (k in 0:10) {
      real pk = rect(poisson_cdf(k | lh), k > 0 ? poisson_cdf(k - 1 | lh) : 0, poisson_cdf(k | la), k > 0 ? poisson_cdf(k - 1 | la) : 0, theta);
      real pind = exp(poisson_lpmf(k | lh) + poisson_lpmf(k | la));
      p_draw += pk / N; p_draw_ind += pind / N;
      if (k == 0) { p00 += pk / N; p00_ind += pind / N; }
      if (k == 1) { p11 += pk / N; p11_ind += pind / N; }
    }
  }
}"
foot_path <- "fits/ch11_foot_frank.rds"
if (file.exists(foot_path)) foot_fit <- readRDS(foot_path) else {
  foot_fit <- stan(model_code = foot_code, chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 11, refresh = 0,
                   data = list(N = nrow(epl), T = length(teams), hg = epl$hg, ag = epl$ag,
                               ht = match(paste(epl$season, epl$home), teams), at = match(paste(epl$season, epl$away), teams)))
  saveRDS(foot_fit, foot_path) }
summary(foot_fit, pars = c("theta", "home", "s_att", "s_def"), probs = c(0.05, 0.95))$summary[, c("mean", "5%", "95%", "Rhat")] |> round(3)
lam <- rstan::extract(foot_fit, c("lam_h", "lam_a"))
c(divergences = get_num_divergent(foot_fit),
  cor_of_expected_goals = round(cor(colMeans(lam$lam_h), colMeans(lam$lam_a)), 3))
pred <- summary(foot_fit, pars = c("p_draw", "p_draw_ind", "p00", "p00_ind", "p11", "p11_ind"), probs = c(0.05, 0.95))$summary[, c("mean", "5%", "95%")]
cbind(observed = c(rep(mean(epl$hg == epl$ag), 2), rep(mean(epl$hg == 0 & epl$ag == 0), 2), rep(mean(epl$hg == 1 & epl$ag == 1), 2)), pred) |> round(4)
output

The raw scores are negatively correlated (−0.15), but most of that is team strength: across matches, the model's expected home and away goals correlate −0.54, because a strong team both scores more and concedes less. Given the strengths, the Frank parameter is θ=−0.28 (90% interval −0.51 to −0.04), a Kendall's τ of −0.03: weak negative dependence within a match, with no divergent transitions and R^≤1.002. Where does it show? Independence predicts that 6.5% of matches end 0–0 (90% interval 6.1% to 6.8%), the copula 6.0% (5.5% to 6.6%), and 5.4% did, so the copula moves toward the data. But it also lowers the predicted share of all draws, from 23.1% to 22.5% (22.0% to 23.2%), while 23.0% of matches were drawn, and both models predict 1–1 at 10.5% against 11.1% observed. Dixon and Coles (1997), with English league matches from the 1990s, found the opposite adjustment, more low-scoring draws than independence predicts, and McHale and Scarf (2011), modelling international matches with copulas, found dependence that was weak between evenly matched teams and increasingly negative as matches became less competitive. In the modern Premier League, conditional on the teams' strengths, home and away goals are close to independent, and the small dependence there is cannot be summarised as "more draws". That is a useful negative result: the independence assumption of the Afterword's model survived a check that could have refuted it, and a copula on conditional margins is how the check is done.

Project Connections: Dependence Beyond Correlation

For the cancer gene-expression project, Section 11.13 is a template: co-amplified genes are tail-dependent, not just correlated, and a copula on pairs (or a vine copula, which builds a high-dimensional copula from a tree of bivariate ones; Aas et al., 2009) describes pathway structure that a correlation network misses. For the quantum computing project of the Afterword, the question "do qubits on one device have bad days together?" is a question about upper tail dependence of error rates, and it decides whether choosing qubits independently is safe; fit the copula to the residuals of the state-space model, not to the raw rates, for the same reason as in Section 11.15. For the student evaluation and exam anxiety projects, the semiparametric Gaussian copula of Section 11.14 is the right way to correlate Likert items with grades, ages and indicators, and the Gaussian copula factor model is the right way to measure anxiety from them. For NYC EMS response equity, daily average response times in the five boroughs rise together on bad days (snowstorms, heat waves, holidays), and a copula with upper tail dependence fitted to the daily series describes how often the whole city is stretched at once. For football, Section 11.15 is the check every goals model should report, and the same rectangle likelihood extends to shots, corners and cards. For AI-generated text detection, detectors combine many features as if they were independent given the author; a Gaussian copula on the features, fitted separately for each author type, is the simplest way to stop correlated evidence being counted twice, the failing of naive Bayes in Chapter 12.

Research Practice: Reporting a Copula Model

  • Say how the margins were handled: modelled jointly, estimated first and plugged in, or replaced by ranks. The last two understate uncertainty; say so.
  • Report the family comparison (LOO or held-out log likelihood, with standard errors), including at least one family with tail dependence in each tail that the question involves, and show the data's corners next to the fitted copula's.
  • Report dependence as Kendall's τ and, when extremes matter, as tail dependence or a joint exceedance probability with an interval, not only as the family's own parameter, which is not comparable across families.
  • For discrete or mixed data, state how ties were handled (the rectangle likelihood or the extended rank likelihood), and never apply a continuous-data method to ranks with many ties.
  • Fit the copula to conditional margins when predictors explain part of the dependence, as team strength does for goals.

History: Links Between Margins

Wassily Hoeffding (1940) and Maurice Fréchet (1951) found the bounds of Section 11.11 while studying joint distributions with given margins. Abe Sklar (1959) proved the theorem and named the object, from the Latin copula, a link or tie, in a three-page note written in answer to a question of Fréchet's. For two decades copulas were mostly a topic in probabilistic metric spaces, until statisticians, starting with Christian Genest and Jock MacKay's "The joy of copulas" (1986), recognised them as a way to build multivariate models. Harry Joe (1997, 2014) and Roger Nelsen (2006) wrote the standard texts; Kjersti Aas and colleagues (2009) made vine copulas practical in high dimensions; and Peter Hoff's extended rank likelihood (2007) gave a fully Bayesian treatment of mixed data. Copulas spread through actuarial science, hydrology and finance, where joint extremes are the whole problem, and, after 2008, into the cautionary tales of finance.

Key Takeaways: Lecture 23

  • A copula is the joint distribution of the ranks: by Sklar's theorem, any continuous joint distribution splits uniquely into its margins and a copula, and any copula combines with any margins.
  • Kendall's τ and Spearman's ρS depend only on the copula; Pearson's correlation does not, and some correlations are unattainable for given margins.
  • Families with the same τ differ in their tails: Gaussian and Frank have no tail dependence, Clayton has lower, Gumbel upper, t both. For co-amplified ERBB2 and GRB7 a Gumbel copula beat the Gaussian by 87.5 in LOO, but the data's tails are those of a mixture of subtypes: check joint exceedances at thresholds the data support, and do not trust a fitted λ beyond them.
  • Bayesian copula models can use the full likelihood (margins and copula together) or ranks as pseudo-observations; for mixed and ordinal data, the Gaussian copula with Hoff's extended rank likelihood recovers latent correlations that Pearson's attenuates.
  • For discrete outcomes the likelihood is a rectangle probability. In the Premier League, the raw negative correlation of home and away goals comes from team strength; given the strengths, the scores are close to independent.

11.16 Exercises

Each exercise has a hint and an answer button.

Exercises

  1. What five factors miss. For the five-factor model, compute the residual correlations: observed item correlations minus those implied by the posterior mean of ΛΛ⊤+Ψ. Which item pairs are worst fitted, and how many of the 300 pairs have residuals larger than 0.1 in absolute value?

    cov2cor(Lm %*% t(Lm) + diag(psi^2)) gives the implied correlations.

    The five-factor model reproduces the correlations well: only one of the 300 item pairs has a residual correlation above 0.1 in absolute value, A1 with A2 (0.123), and 25 exceed 0.05. The worst-fitted pairs are A1–A2, A1–C4 (0.085), E1–A1 (0.079), N3–N4 (0.076), C4–O5 (0.075) and O2–O5 (0.072). Several involve reverse-scored items (A1, C4, E1, O2, O5): negatively worded statements share a little variance of their own, a well-known "method factor" in questionnaire data, and one candidate for what the sixth factor of Section 11.5 picks up.

  2. Factor scores. Compute each person's estimated factor scores, f^i=Λ⊤Σ−1yi, from the posterior means, and compare women and men on each factor in standard-deviation units (in bfi, gender is 1 for men and 2 for women). Is this a causal comparison?

    Keep only the rows used in the fit (complete.cases(bfi[, 1:25])).

    The data contain 805 men and 1,631 women. In standard-deviation units, women score higher than men on Agreeableness (0.40), Neuroticism (0.27), Conscientiousness (0.19) and Extraversion (0.15), and lower on Openness (−0.25). These differences are descriptive, not causal: the sample is self-selected volunteers on a website, the comparison mixes everything that differs between women and men in this sample (age, education, culture of response), and it assumes the items measure the same traits in the same way for both groups (measurement invariance), which should itself be tested by fitting the factor model separately or jointly with group-specific loadings.

  3. Bayesian versus classical. Compare the posterior mean loadings with the maximum-likelihood varimax solution from factanal(), after aligning the two by a Procrustes rotation. How different are they, and why?

    Align with the singular value decomposition of ΛML⊤ΛBayes, as in rotate_draws().

    After alignment, the largest difference between the Bayesian posterior means and the maximum-likelihood loadings is 0.003 (mean 0.0009), against posterior standard deviations of up to 0.024. With 2,436 people and weak priors, the likelihood dominates and the two methods agree; the Bayesian fit adds uncertainty for every loading and every derived quantity (communalities, factor scores, residual correlations), and it would matter more with a few hundred respondents or with informative priors on the loadings.

  4. Simpler groups. Refit the three-group penguin mixture with diagonal covariance matrices (each measurement independent within a group). How well does it recover the species, and how does it compare with the full-covariance model by PSIS-LOO?

    Replace multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf by normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[k], sigma[k]) and drop Omega.

    The diagonal model is both worse and harder to fit. Its chains split: three reached an average log density near −1404 and one −1385, so align_chains() keeps only the last. That chain's solution puts all Adélie and Chinstrap penguins in one group and splits the Gentoo into two (61 and 62 birds, very likely by sex). By PSIS-LOO it is far worse than the full-covariance model (difference −174.7, standard error 22.6). The reason is that bill length, bill depth, flipper length and mass are strongly correlated within each species (bigger birds are bigger everywhere); a diagonal model can only represent that correlation by adding groups along the size axis, which is exactly what it did with the Gentoo.

  5. k-means. Run k-means with three clusters on the standardised penguin measurements. How does it compare with the species, and with the mixture's most probable groups? What does k-means implicitly assume that the mixture does not?

    kmeans(Yp, 3, nstart = 50).

    k-means puts all 123 Gentoo together, but it assigns 24 Adélie to the Chinstrap cluster (and 5 Chinstrap to the Adélie cluster), so 29 penguins are grouped with another species, against 6 for the mixture; the two methods disagree about 23 birds. k-means implicitly fits a mixture with equal weights and the same spherical covariance in every group, and assigns each point wholly to the nearest centre. Adélie are far more numerous than Chinstrap and their clouds are elongated and correlated, so equal spheres misplace the boundary; and k-means gives no measure of how borderline each assignment is.

  6. More components of expression. Repeat the TCGA analysis of Section 11.9 with the first five principal components instead of three. Do the groups match the subtypes better?

    Use fit_mix() or the same sampling() call with D=5.

    With five components the groups match the subtypes somewhat better, and differently. The Basal group is unchanged (132 of 141). The other two groups now split along a new line: one group holds 62 of the 67 HER2-enriched tumours, with 41 Luminal B, 16 Luminal A, 9 Basal and 6 Normal-like, so HER2-enriched tumours are its largest class but under half of it; the other holds 405 of the 421 Luminal A and 151 of the 192 Luminal B tumours, which are no longer separated at all. The chains agree (log densities within 1 unit). Only 116 of the 844 tumours are now uncertain, against 279 with three components, and the adjusted Rand index with the PAM50 calls rises from 0.42 to 0.49. More components capture more biology, but with three groups the mixture must choose which division to show, and it shows whichever the reduction makes largest; the Luminal A and B distinction lost out here. The number of components is a modelling choice to report, not a nuisance detail.

  7. A prior on the number of groups. Under a Dirichlet process with α=1, what is the prior expected number of groups among the 342 penguins? What value of α makes the expectation 3? With that α, what is the expectation for 10,000 penguins?

    E[Kn]=∑i=1nα/(α+i−1); solve for α with uniroot().

    With α=1 the prior expects 6.41 groups among 342 penguins, already twice the number of species. Setting the expectation to 3 requires α≈0.335; with that α, the expected number of groups among 10,000 penguins is 4.13. The logarithmic growth means a prior tuned to one sample size gives a different expected number of groups at another, which is why the concentration parameter is often given its own prior rather than fixed.

  8. Bad anchors. Refit the five-factor model with the hand-picked anchors N1, E4, C2, A2 and O1 and Stan's default random initial values (four chains). Report each chain's posterior mean of the five diagonal loadings and the largest R^. What went wrong, or right?

    Reorder the columns of Y so that the anchors come first, and call sampling() without init.

    Three chains agree, and one does not. The anchors' diagonal loadings are 0.86, 0.72, 0.65, 0.41 and 0.50 in chains 1 to 3, but chain 4 has 0.01 for the fourth anchor (A2) and 0.23 for the fifth (O1), and the largest R^ is 8.2. The fourth chain settled in a mode where A2 does not define its own factor: the factor that should be Agreeableness has taken a different direction, with A2's loading forced to be positive but almost zero. A2 was a weak anchor, because it also loads on Extraversion. The fix used in Section 11.4 (anchors chosen from a classical solution, and chains started there) is not cosmetic; without it, the model is identified in theory but multimodal in practice.

  9. Unattainable correlations. Let X be lognormal(0, 1) and Y lognormal(0, σ2) with σ=2. Using the Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds, find the largest and smallest Pearson correlations the pair can have, whatever their copula. Check by simulation. What does this say about specifying a joint distribution by margins and a correlation matrix?

    The bounds are attained by Y=eσZ and Y=e−σZ with X=eZ, Z standard normal. Use E[eaZ]=ea2/2 to show that the correlation is (e±σ−1)/(e−1)(eσ2−1).

    The largest attainable correlation is (e2−1)/(e−1)(e4−1)=0.666 and the smallest (e−2−1)/(e−1)(e4−1)=−0.090, even though in the first case Y is an increasing function of X and in the second a decreasing one. A simulation of a million pairs gives 0.717 and −0.095: the sample correlation of such skewed variables converges slowly, which is a second warning about using it. So a correlation of 0.8 between these two variables is impossible, and "perfect dependence" can show up as a correlation of 0.67. A correlation matrix with given margins may not correspond to any joint distribution, and, when it does, it does not determine one; the copula, with τ or ρS as the summary, has neither problem.

  10. The Gaussian copula's vanishing tail. For the Gaussian and Gumbel copulas fitted to ERBB2 and GRB7 (posterior mean parameters), compute Pr(V>q∣U>q) for q = 0.9, 0.99, 0.999 and 0.9999. What happens as q→1?

    Pr(V>q∣U>q)=(1−2q+C(q,q))/(1−q); use pCopula(c(q, q), normalCopula(rho)) for the Gaussian and C(q,q)=q21/θ for the Gumbel.

    With ρ=0.727 the Gaussian copula gives 0.49, 0.29, 0.18 and 0.12: the conditional probability keeps falling, toward its limit of λU=0, although very slowly (for a Gaussian copula the decay is roughly a power of 1−q). The Gumbel copula with θ=2.20 gives 0.66, 0.63, 0.63 and 0.63, settling at λU=2−21/θ=0.63. At the 90th percentile the two differ by a third; at one in ten thousand by a factor of five. Data with a thousand observations cannot tell which limit is right, so the choice of family is an assumption about how extremes behave beyond the data, and it should be reported as one.

  11. A mixture of copulas. Split the tumours by clinical HER2 status (HER2_Final_Status_nature2012 in the clinical file of Chapter 10). Compute Kendall's τ of ERBB2 and GRB7 within the positive and the negative tumours, and count the HER2-positive tumours among those in the top 10%, 5% and 2% of both genes. How does this explain the shape of the observed curve in the widget of Section 11.13?

    Join the clinical file to G by tumour; for the counts, use the pseudo-observations computed from all tumours.

    Within the 114 HER2-positive tumours τ=0.73; within the 652 negative ones τ=0.35. Of the 102 tumours in the top 10% of both genes, 75 are positive, 2 negative and 25 have no recorded status; of the 43 in the top 5%, 28 are positive and 1 negative. The pooled data are a mixture: a large group with moderate dependence, and a group of about one tumour in seven whose amplified genes sit above everyone else's. Being in the top 10% of one gene almost guarantees membership of the amplified group, and hence being in the top 10% of the other, which is why the observed conditional probability peaks near 0.94 at q=0.9, roughly where the amplified group begins. Further into the tail we are ranking tumours within the amplified group, where the dependence is strong but not perfect (Kendall's τ is 0.59 among the top 10% of ERBB2), so the curve falls. A model with a latent subgroup and a copula within each, the mixture of Lecture 22 with copula components, would reproduce both features; any single one-parameter family must compromise.

  12. Polychoric correlations. For the five Neuroticism items, compare the latent correlations of Section 11.14 with the polychoric correlations from psych::polychoric() and with Pearson's correlations of the codes. Why do the first two agree?

    psych::polychoric(D[, 1:5])$rho.

    The polychoric and copula correlations agree to within 0.004 for all ten pairs (for example 0.764 and 0.767 for N1 and N2, 0.437 and 0.440 for N1 and N4), while Pearson's are 0.03 to 0.06 lower (0.707 and 0.398). A polychoric correlation is the correlation of a bivariate normal distribution whose thresholds reproduce the observed table of two ordinal items, which is exactly the Gaussian copula model for a pair of ordinal variables; estimated by maximum likelihood with thresholds fixed from the margins, it is the classical version of the same estimate. The Bayesian copula adds three things: it handles ordinal, binary and continuous variables in one model rather than pair by pair, so the matrix is guaranteed to be a valid correlation matrix; it imputes missing values; and it gives posterior intervals.

  13. Low scores. Using the posterior means of the expected goals and of θ from Section 11.15, compute the expected number of matches ending in each score from 0–0 to 2–2 under independence and under the Frank copula, and compare with the observed counts. Which discrepancies could a copula fix?

    Sum the rectangle probabilities over the 2,280 matches; under independence the probability of x–y is dpois(x, lh) * dpois(y, la).

    Observed, independent and Frank counts are: 0–0, 123, 140 and 130; 1–0, 200, 201 and 197; 0–1, 158, 177 and 175; 1–1, 252, 244 and 245; 2–0, 157, 157 and 161; 0–2, 136, 121 and 126; 2–1, 187, 183 and 184; 1–2, 157, 161 and 163; 2–2, 125, 115 and 113. The copula moves the 0–0 count halfway to the data and changes little else. The other discrepancies, such as too few 0–1 results and too many 0–2 and 2–2 results, are not of the form a single dependence parameter can fix; with counts of this size the Poisson standard deviation is about 12 to 14, so none is more than about 1.5 standard deviations from either model. The check supports independence given team strengths; if a larger data set confirmed a pattern like the 0–1 deficit, the margins (for example overdispersion, or scoring that depends on the current score) would be the place to look, not the copula.

Further reading and references

Further Reading

  • Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), Chapters 9 and 12: mixtures, EM and probabilistic PCA, with clear derivations.
  • Frühwirth-Schnatter, Celeux and Robert (eds.), Handbook of Mixture Analysis (2019): the modern reference for finite mixtures, label switching and choosing K.
  • Betancourt's case study "Identifying Bayesian mixture models" (2017, on the Stan website): why mixtures are hard for HMC, shown with care.
  • Borsboom, Mellenbergh and van Heerden, "The theoretical status of latent variables" (2003): what it means to say a factor causes test scores.
  • Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition, 2013), Chapters 22 and 23: finite mixtures and Dirichlet process models.
  • Nelsen, An Introduction to Copulas (2nd edition, 2006): the gentlest rigorous introduction, with Sklar's theorem, the families and the dependence measures; Joe, Dependence Modeling with Copulas (2014) is the comprehensive reference, including vines.
  • Genest and Nešlehová, "A primer on copulas for count data" (2007): what goes wrong with discrete margins, and why.
  • Hoff, "Extending the rank likelihood for semiparametric copula estimation" (2007): the Gaussian copula for mixed data, short and readable.
